Critical Apparatus Removed ## Part 1. Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter 1 (Bd. I. 3.1—38; Kū. 4.6—66; L. 70.3—66; Mr. 45.29—73; Vā. 4.5—92.)
Listen to this divine narrative, which liberates one from all sins—wondrous, rich in meaning, and in accord with the Vedas—as it is being told by me! || 1 ||
Whoever should constantly uphold this, or listen to it repeatedly,
or likewise cause it to be heard by Brahmins and especially by ascetics— pure-hearted, self-disciplined, on the sacred festival days, at holy fords and shrines—
One attains a long life by reciting this ancient narrative. || 2 ||
Having ensured the continuation of his own lineage, he is glorified in the heavenly world. || 2 ||
Listen as I proclaim the detailed accounts of those ancestors, exactly as they occurred and as they were heard, which increase their glory. (3)
The recounting of the deeds of all those of meritorious action, whose fame is steadfast, brings wealth, renown, the destruction of enemies, heavenly merit, and an increase in longevity.
Cosmogony, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the accounts of the dynasties—thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics. || 4 ||

Because it is fashioned through the Kalpas, it is called the Kalpa. Indeed, that Kalpa which is even beyond all Kalpas, which is entirely pure for the sake of purity, and which is fixedly pure for those who are pure—that ancient Purāṇa, equal to the Veda, I shall proclaim, O Māruti. || 4 ||
Awakening, dissolution, maintenance, and indeed origination—this is the first chapter, which comprises the exposition of the subject matter. || 4 ||
The introduction, the continuation, and the conclusion—[which is righteous, conducive to fame, conducive to long life, and the destroyer of all sins]. (4)
Thus, these four feet have been briefly proclaimed by me;
I shall, however, explain them again in detail according to their sequence. || 45 ||
Having bowed down to that wise Hiranyagarbha, the sustainer of the worlds, I shall speak correctly.
The unsurpassed creation of beings. || 5 ||
Beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), it possesses various forms and characteristics;
it is accessible through the five means of valid cognition and endowed with six streams. || 6 ||
It is eternally presided over by the Puruṣa,
yet it appears as if non-eternal;
listen to that, O highly fortunate one.
By means of the supreme meditative concentration. || 7 ||
That which is the primary cause,
the great seers call it by the name "Unmanifest" (avyakta), which they also term the subtle primordial nature (prakṛti).
Eternal, consisting of both being and non-being. || 8 ||
It is eternal, imperishable, undecaying,
immeasurable, not dependent on anything else, and devoid of smell, form, and taste.
Devoid of sound and touch! || 9 ||
To that Hiranyagarbha, the Puruṣa, and the Īśvara,
who is indeed the first Unborn One.
Having paid homage to the self-existent Brahmā, the most excellent creator of beings and the sustainer of the worlds, || 5 ||
That which consists of five means of knowledge, six streams, and is presided over by the Puruṣa; || 6 ||
I shall describe up to the point of restraint the unsurpassed creation of beings;
that which is the unmanifest cause—
It is eternal, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
That which the seekers of truth call Pradhāna and Prakṛti is devoid of smell, color, and taste.
Devoid of sound and touch. || 8 ||
The source of the world, the great element, which is undecaying, firm, inexhaustible, eternal, and established in its own self.
The eternal Supreme Brahman,
the embodiment of all beings,
indeed became unmanifest. || 9 ||
Without beginning or end, unborn, subtle, consisting of the three qualities, the source and the place of dissolution, incomparable and unknowable, Brahman existed first. || 10 ||
Following that dissolution, this [universe] was pervaded by it in its entirety;
because of the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), from that [state], it [arose].
O Sage, from that [unmanifest], presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
creation proceeds again at the time of emanation through the manifestation of the qualities (guṇas).
The manifested principle of Pradhāna enveloped that Mahat. || 12 ||
Just as a seed is covered by its husk, so too is the Great Principle (mahat) veiled by the unmanifest;
it is likewise composed of the qualities of sattva and rajas.
And the tamasic [nature] is said to be threefold. || 13 ||
All this was pervaded by his own self, consisting of darkness;
at that time, there was an equilibrium of the qualities within him.
At the time of creation, when the primary matter (pradhāna), presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), exists in an undifferentiated state consisting of darkness (tamas).
Being manifested through the state of being a subordinate quality (guṇabhāva),
the Great One (Mahat) indeed appeared;
then, by means of that subtle and great [principle], he [appeared].
Enveloped by the unmanifest. || 12 ||
In the beginning, the Great One (mahat) is predominant in sattva and manifests as pure sattva; it should be understood that both the mind (manas) and the Great One are [of this nature].
That single cause is traditionally taught. || 13 ||
The Great Principle (mahat) arises as a mere subtle sign presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
and [it manifests] forms such as dharma and the rest, which are the causes for the true purpose of the world. || 14 ||
Volition and determination are known as its two functions.
Urged by the desire to create, the Great One (Mahat) effects the transformation of creation.
It is called mind (manas), the Great One (mahat), thought (mati), Brahmā, the Full (pūr), intellect (buddhi), renown (khyāti), and the Lord (īśvara). (15)
Wisdom is called the altar, mindfulness is consciousness, and it is termed the triple city by the wise;
for the all-pervading Lord, as the mind, perceives the activity and its fruit of all living beings. (16)

Because it is subtle for those who have awakened [to it], it is therefore called "mind" (manas). Since it is the first-born among the principles (tattvas) and is great in its dimension, [it is so named]. (17)
After the remaining principles of the qualities (guṇatattva), it is known as Mahat;
it maintains the sense of measurement, it conceives, and it also effects differentiation. || 18 ||
The person (puruṣa) is so called because of his connection with experience; by that [connection], this intellect (mati) is traditionally known [as such].
Furthermore, it is called "Brahman" because of its vastness, its capacity to nourish all things, and because it is the substratum of all states of being. (19)
Because he causes all things to flourish, he is therefore defined as Brahmā;
and because he fills all bodies with his favors. || 20 ||
And because it is the locus of the determined states of reality (*tattvabhāva*), it is called "the city" (*pura*);
and herein the *puruṣa* perceives all things, both beneficial and harmful. || 21 ||
Because it causes one to awaken, it is therefore defined as "intellect" (buddhi);
because from it proceeds both manifestation and individual experience, it is so called. || 22 ||
Because enjoyment is grounded in knowledge, it is therefore remembered as "manifestation" (khyāti).
Or rather, it is manifested manifoldly through its qualities, such as names and so forth. || 23 ||
And because of that greatness, he is designated by the name "Khyāti" (Renown).
The Great-Souled One perceives everything directly; for that reason, he is the Lord (Īśvara). || 24 ||
Because he is born from that [wisdom], he is therefore called "Prājña" (the Wise).
Furthermore, the forms such as knowledge and the like, as well as the fruits of sacrificial acts, [arise from him]. || 25 ||
Because it accumulates for the sake of experience, it is therefore called "citi" (the accumulator);
[it gathers] those that are present, as well as those that are past and likewise those that are yet to come. (26)
Because it remembers all duties, it is called *smṛti* (tradition/memory);
and because it attains complete knowledge, it is called *mahātmya* (greatness). || 27 ||
Therefore, "to find" (vindati) and "to know" (veda) are both designated as "consciousness" (saṃvit).
That consciousness is found in everything, and everything is found within it. || 28 ||
Therefore, he is called "Consciousness" (saṃvit) by those who are truly highly intelligent.
Because he is knowledge itself, the Blessed One, the treasury of knowledge, calls him "Knowledge.
Because he effects the dissolution of dualities, he is called "Vipura" by the wise. || 29 ||
Because he is the lord of all worlds, he is necessarily the Īśvara;
because of his vastness, he is remembered as Brahmā; and because he has come into being, he is called Bhava. || 20 ||
Because of his knowledge of the field and the knower of the field, and because of his oneness, who is he remembered as? Because he dwells within the city [of the body], he is called the Puruṣa;
because he is not produced and because he is primordial, he is called the Self-Existent (Svayambhū). || 29 ||
The primordial and unsurpassed reality has been explained by those who know the true nature of things and contemplate the true being of the God, using words that express the path. || 30 ||
From that, indeed, the threefold ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) was born: the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and [the Bhūtādi].
And he, being characterized by tamas, [created] the elements and so forth. || 31 ||
And that Mahat, being enveloped by the manifest,
indeed transforms the creation, just as Mahat itself does.
Being impelled by the desire to emit [the world],
its two functions are traditionally held to be volition (saṃkalpa) and determination (adhyavasāya). || 30 ||
Furthermore, forms such as dharma and the rest are the causes for the purpose of the reality of the world; that [reality], however,
should be understood as consisting of the three guṇas.
[The intellect] characterized by goodness, passion, and darkness. || 31 ||
From the triple-guṇa [principle], when rajas was predominant, ego (ahaṃkāra) arose from that;
this creation is enveloped by the Great One (mahat).
But externally, it consists of the elements and so forth. || 31 ||
And from that ego (ahaṃkāra) in which darkness (tamas) predominates, there arose the creation of the subtle elements (tanmātra) of the gross elements (bhūta).
But that which consists of the elements and so forth is tamasic. || 31 ||
Then the primary element (bhūtādi), undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) from that [state].
From the subtle element of sound, [the ether was produced].
Space has sound as its defining characteristic. || 32 ||
Space, which is merely sound, then again envelops the source of the elements (bhūtādi);
from that, the subtle element of touch alone is born here—of this there is no doubt. || 33 ||
The powerful wind is born; touch is considered its quality.
And the wind, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of form (rūpamātra);
light arises from the wind, and it is said to have form as its quality. || 35 ||
But the wind, consisting of the subtle element of touch alone, enveloped the subtle element of form;
and light, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of taste. || 36 ||
From that, indeed, the waters arise; they consist of all tastes.
Those waters, being merely taste, were enveloped by fire, which consists of mere form. || 37 ||
The waters also, undergoing transformation, produced mere fragrance;
from that, the aggregate (saṃghāta) is born, and fragrance is considered its quality. || 38 ||

That water, being merely taste, enveloped the mere smell; because it is a "mere" (tanmātra) element in each respective case, it is known as a "subtle element" (tanmātra); and because they denote that which is without distinction, they are therefore called "undifferentiated" (aviśeṣa). || 39 ||
They are neither peaceful nor terrible, neither deluded nor undifferentiated;
this is the creation of the elements and the subtle elements.
But from the tamasic ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 40 ||
From the *vaikārika* ego, which is characterized by the predominance of *sattva*, that *vaikārika* creation proceeds simultaneously. || 41 ||
There are exactly five sense organs and five organs of action;

they say these are the Taijasa (fiery) organs. The ten Vaikārika (evolvent) deities are the instruments that accomplish [the functions of] the organs. || 42 || The ten Vaikārika deities are [the presiding deities of the organs]. || 42 ||
The eleventh there is the mind; the gods are known as the Vaikārikas.
The ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth [are the organs of perception]. (43)
For the sake of attaining sound and the other objects of sense, those endowed with intelligence will be described.
The feet, the anus, the generative organ, the hands, and speech shall be the fifth. || 44 ||
Movement, emission, bliss, craftsmanship, and speech—these are its functions.
Space, being merely sound, then entered into the mere element of touch. || 45 ||
Twofold from that, however, arose the wind, consisting of sound and touch;
likewise, form entered into those two qualities of sound and touch. || 46 ||
From that, fire arises, consisting of the three qualities; it possesses sound, touch, and form.
Sound, touch, and form enter into the subtle element of taste. || 47 ||
Therefore, water, which consists of the essence of taste, should be known as possessing four qualities;
for sound, touch, form, and taste enter into it, along with smell. || 48 ||
Being joined with even a mere scent, they cover this entire earth;
therefore, among the elements, earth is declared to be gross, possessing five qualities. || 49 ||
They are known as the specific qualities—tranquil, terrible, and deluded—and because they mutually interpenetrate, they sustain one another. (50)

All this, up to the end of the earth, is enveloped by the Lokaloka mountain; furthermore, the specific objects are those perceivable by the senses, and they are so designated because of their fixed nature. || 51 ||
Each subsequent one acquires the quality of each preceding one.
Whatever [the number] of those [qualities] there may be, each one is said to possess that many times as many qualities. || 52 ||

If some were to perceive a fragrance in water and claim it to be a quality of water, one should know that it actually belongs to the earth, [present there] due to its contact with water and air. || 52 ||
These seven, possessing diverse powers and being separate from one another, were unable to create living beings without a collective union.
Having come together in mutual conjunction,
they are dependent upon one another and bear the mark of a single composite whole.
Having attained complete unity in its entirety. || 54 ||
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest, those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg. || 55 ||
O one of great intelligence, from those elements an egg gradually grew, like a bubble upon the water.
That vast one dwells within the waters. || 56 ||
At that time, the accomplishment of the task was fully realized by Brahmā;
for when the elemental egg had expanded, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) was designated as Brahmā. || 57 ||
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called Puruṣa.
As the original creator of all beings, Brahmā appeared at the beginning. || 58 ||
By him all this triple world, including the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded. || 59 ||
Meru became his amnion and the mountains his chorion;
the oceans were the fetal waters of that Supreme Self. || 60 ||
Within that egg was the entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans,
as well as the continents, mountains, and oceans.
As long as the light lasts is the gathering of people. || 61 ||
Then the egg is surrounded on the outside by water, wind, fire, and space, and by the *bhūtādi* [tattva], each ten times the size of the preceding.
Furthermore, by means of each one of those individually. || 64 ||
He was enveloped together with that great one of the same measure;
the Great One, accompanied by all of them.
Enveloped by the unmanifest. || 65 ||
The egg is enveloped by these seven elemental coverings;
having mutually enveloped one another, these eight constitute that eternal Prakṛti.
And that Person within it is the one called Brahman whom I have described to you;
hear it again in brief. || 65 ||
Just as someone submerged in water, upon emerging,
splashes the water born from the water; so too does Brahmā.
He is thus the all-pervading primordial nature. || 66 ||

The Unmanifest is designated as the field (kṣetra), and Brahmā is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña); one should understand this entire definition of the field and the knower of the field. || 67 ||
Thus, this is the primary creation; presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), it appeared first without prior conscious intent, like a flash of lightning. || 68 ||
He who knows this birth of Hiraṇyagarbha in its true essence becomes long-lived, famous, fortunate, and possessed of progeny. || 68 ||
Even a man who desires liberation, being pure in soul, attains the goal through constant listening to the Purāṇas; he shall obtain happiness and security. || 68 ||

**Chapter 2: Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation** O twice-born ones, that duration of time which has been calculated by me for the period of emission (*visṛṣṭi*)—this very duration of time should be known as one day of the Supreme Lord. || 1 ||
The entire night of the Supreme Lord should be known as being of this same duration;
his day, however, is the creation, while dissolution is called his night. || 2 ||
For him, there is neither day nor night—this is the firm conviction;
yet, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, conventional designations are employed. || 3 ||
[The subjects, the lords of creatures, the seers along with the sages, and the seers known as Sanatkumāra together with those who have attained union with Brahman. || 3 ||
The sense organs and the objects of the senses, the five great elements, the subtle elements, the group of sense organs, the intellect, together with the mind; || 4 ||
All these remain during the day of the wise Supreme Lord; at the end of the day they are dissolved, and at the end of the night the origin of the universe [reappears]. || 5 ||
When the manifest has subsided into its own self and modification has been withdrawn, both Pradhāna and Puruṣa remain in a state of similarity. || 6 ||
These two qualities, darkness (tamas) and goodness (sattva), existed in a state of equilibrium;
unmixed yet interwoven with one another. || 7 ||
When there is equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), dissolution is to be known; when there is disequilibrium, creation is said to occur.
Just as oil exists in sesame seeds, or as clarified butter resides in milk. || 8 ||
Likewise, while darkness (tamas) and goodness (sattva) remain supported by the unmanifest (avyakta), Rajas remains present;
at that time, one should worship the supreme, divine Night of Maheśvara throughout its entirety.
And when the break of day had arrived, the Supreme Lord, by means of his supreme yoga, caused the other [Purusha], who was born of Prakriti, to be agitated. || 10 ||
Having entered both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, Maheśvara caused agitation to arise from Pradhāna, and from that agitated state, indeed,
Rajas came into being.
In that regard, rajas is the activator, just as water is for seeds. || 11 ||
Having reached an imbalance of the qualities (guṇa),
they are indeed brought forth when presided over by the Unmanifest;
for from the qualities being agitated, [the world arises].
Three gods were born. || 11 ||
From Maheśvara, the Lord of the World, three gods were born. || 11 ||
They are eternal, supremely secret, the self of all, and embodied beings. || 12 ||
Rajas is Brahmā, tamas is indeed Agni, and sattva was born as Viṣṇu;
rajas is the illuminator, and Brahmā is established in his role as the creator. || 12 ||
Agni, who illuminates darkness, is established as Time; Viṣṇu, who illuminates the quality of goodness (sattva), is established in neutrality. || 12 ||
These indeed are the three worlds; these indeed are the three qualities;
these indeed are the three Vedas; these indeed are the three fires. || 13 ||
For these are mutually dependent, following one another;
they exist through one another and support one another. || 14 ||
For these are indeed joined in mutual union and depend upon one another for their livelihood;
there is never even a moment's separation among them, nor do they ever abandon each other. || 15 ||
For Īśvara is the supreme deity, while Viṣṇu is beyond Mahat;
Brahmā, however, being overflowing with the quality of rajas, proceeds here for the sake of creation.
Puruṣa is to be known as the highest, and Prakṛti is remembered as the supreme. || 16 ||
For he, being presided over by Maheśvara, proceeds when impelled from all sides;
and the great ones, having long endured, follow him because of their affection for their own domain. || 17 ||
At the time of creation, the Pradhāna proceeds from the inequality of its qualities;
it is presided over by Īśvara, and it consists of both the existent and the non-existent. || 18 ||
Brahmā and Buddhi arose simultaneously as a couple;
from that [arose] Tamas, the unmanifest Māyā, and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) designated as Brahmā. || 181 ||
Perfected in the performance of his task, he appeared before Brahmā;
matchless in splendor, wise, unmanifest, yet the illuminator of all. || 19 ||

He is indeed the first embodied being, established in the state of causality; he is endowed with unimpeded knowledge and sovereignty, and is fully possessed of unimpeded dharma and detachment. || 20 ||

The knowledge of that Lord is unimpeded and characterized by dispassion; from him, who was free from pride, there arose the intellect (buddhi) pertaining to Brahmā, produced by the sovereignty over all dharmas. From the Unmanifest (avyakta), there arises for him whatever he desires through his mind.
Because it has been brought under control, because it consists of the three qualities (guṇas), because it is dependent, and by its very nature. || 21 ||
The four-faced one exists in the state of Brahmā, while Antaka (the Ender) becomes Time; the thousand-headed Puruṣa is the third—these are the three states of the Self-born. || 22 ||
Sattva and rajas exist in the state of Brahmā; rajas and tamas in the state of Time (Kāla);
and sattva alone in the state of Puruṣa—such is the operation of the qualities (guṇa) of the Self-born One. || 221 ||
In the state of Brahmā, he creates the worlds; in the state of Time, he also withdraws them. || 23 ||
For while the state of being a person is neutral, there are three states of Prajāpati:
Brahmā, who has the luster of the interior of a lotus; and Kāla, who has the brilliance of natural collyrium. || 24 ||
The Person with lotus-eyes is the form of that Supreme Self;
he appears as one, as two, as three, and again as many. || 25 ||
The Lord of Yoga creates and transforms bodies, endowed with various forms, actions, appearances, and names, through His own power of play. || 26 ||
Because he exists in the world in three ways, he is called the "Three-Guṇa" (Triguṇa);
because he is divided fourfold, he is celebrated as the "Fourfold Manifestation" (Caturvyūha). || 27 ||
Because he attains, because he takes up, because the Lord eats the object of experience, and because his state is constant, he is therefore defined as the Self (ātman). || 28 ||
And because he is all-pervading, the Seer is his embodied self, for he is its Lord;
Viṣṇu is its master over everything because he has entered into all. || 29 ||

The Blessed One (Bhagavān) is so called because of the presence of the *bhaga*; Rāga because he teaches passion (*rāga*); Parama because of his supreme excellence; and he is remembered as *Oṃ* because of his protection (*avana*). || 30 ||

He is omniscient because of his knowledge of all things; he is "all" because everything proceeds from him; and since he is the refuge (ayaṇa) of men (nara), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. || 31 ||
Dividing itself into threefold, it proceeds throughout the three worlds;
by means of these three, it itself creates, devours, and beholds.
In the beginning, he appeared as Hiraṇyagarbha with four faces.
Because he was the first, he is known as Ādideva; because he is unborn, he is remembered as Aja.
Since he protects all creatures, he is therefore remembered as Prajāpati. || 33 ||
Among the gods he is the great god; therefore he is remembered as Mahādeva. And because he is the lord of all worlds and is not subject to anyone else, he is likewise called Īśvara.

He is remembered as Brahmā because of his greatness; he is called Bhūta because he has come into being; he is the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) due to his knowledge of the field; and he is the All-pervading (Vibhu) because he is omnipresent. || 35 ||
Because he dwells within the city (puri), he is called Puruṣa;
and because he is beginningless and primordial, he is remembered as Svayambhū. || 36 ||
He is called Yajña because he is worthy of worship; he is Kavi because his vision is far-reaching;
he is Kramaṇa because he is to be traversed; and he is Pālaka because he protects. || 37 ||
Kapila, the first-born, is known as Āditya-saṃjña and is remembered as Agni;
gold was his embryo, and he was born from the embryo of gold. || 38 ||
Therefore, he is designated as Hiraṇyagarbha in this Purāṇa;
he is the time that follows the cessation of the Self-existent One, occurring at the beginning of the year. || 39 ||
They cannot be fully enumerated even in hundreds of years;
however, a *parārdha* is recorded as being equal to the number of kalpas in the life of Brahmā. || 40 ||
The remainder of his time is yet another; at its conclusion, he is purified.
Indeed, thousands of millions upon millions of intermediate eons are included therein.
Of the eons that have completely passed, there remain others yet to come;
but as for this eon which is currently proceeding, understand it to be the Vārāha.
O twice-born ones, this first eon (kalpa) of theirs is currently proceeding;
during that time, there shall be fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva. || 43 ||
By those who were in the past, those who are present, and those who will indeed be in the future, this entire earth with its seven continents has been [ruled] on all sides. 44.
Indeed, they are to be protected by lords of men for a full thousand yugas, as well as by subjects through austerity; hear now the detailed account of them. || 45 ||
By means of a single Manvantara, all the intermediate periods (Antaras) are indeed described;
and by means of a Kalpa, the future [Kalpas] are likewise described.
One who possesses discernment should apply reasoning to past eons, including their endings and successions, as well as to future ones in the same manner. || 47 ||

## Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter Three There was a terrible, single ocean; for in the beginning, there were only waters, an undifferentiated mass consisting of darkness, when fire had perished from the surface of the earth.
In this [universe] where everything was a single mass with no intervening space, nothing at all could be discerned. || 1 ||
When that world had become a single ocean and all things mobile and immobile had perished,
then Brahmā appeared, possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
The thousand-headed Puruṣa, golden-hued and beyond the senses, known as Brahmā Nārāyaṇa, then slept upon the waters. || 3 ||
But when he was awakened by the predominance of the quality of goodness (sattva), he beheld the world as empty.
And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa: || 4 ||
The waters are called *nārāḥ*,
for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
they are said to be his *ayana* (place of resort).
Therefore, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. || 5 ||
Having remained for a period of night equal to a thousand yugas, at the end of that night,
she brings about the state of Brahmā for the purpose of creation.
Then Brahmā, having become the wind, moved through that water here and there,
like a firefly at night during the rainy season.
Then, having discerned through inference that the earth lay within those waters, he remained undeluded regarding the means of raising it up from the ground.
He assumed another body, just as he had done in former ages at the beginnings of the kalpas;
then that Great-Souled One meditated upon a divine form with his mind.
Seeing the earth submerged on all sides by the waters, he thought:
"In what form shall I assume to lift up this earth? || 10 ||
During his water-sports, he remembered the beautiful form of the Boar, which is invincible to all beings, consisting of speech, and known as Brahman. || 11 ||
Ten yojanas in width and one hundred yojanas in height, resembling a dark blue cloud and sounding like the thundering of clouds. || 11 ||
With the stature of a great mountain, white, possessing horns and fierce tusks, with eyes shining like lightning-fire and splendor equal to the sun. || 11 ||
With broad, rounded, and long shoulders, he walked with the stride of a lion;
his waist was thick and elevated, exceedingly smooth, and endowed with auspicious marks. || 11 ||
Assuming his vast and immeasurable boar-form, Hari entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) for the purpose of uplifting the earth. || 12 ||

He has the Vedas for his feet, the sacrificial post for his tusks, the sacrifice for his chest, and the fire-altar for his mouth; he has Agni for his tongue, Darbha grass for his hair, Brahman for his head, and the great banks [of the rivers] for his hips. || 12 ||
γ cf. 5. kap. sl. 7–8

He has day and night as his eyes, the Vedāṅgas as his ear-ornaments, the clarified butter as his nose, and the sacrificial ladle as his snout; he is great, with the sound of the Sāman chants as his voice. || 122 ||
Consisting of truth and dharma, glorious, established in the valor of dharma, with penance for his claws, terrible, with sacrificial animals for his knees, and of great form— || 123 ||

The Udgātṛ-priest is his intestines; the sacrificial oblation is his characteristic mark; he is the great medicinal herb whose seed is the fruit; the altar is his inner self; the mantra is his buttocks; the clarified butter is his tongue; and the Soma is his blood. || 124 ||
The Veda is his trunk, the fragrance of the oblation is his scent, and he possesses the speed of offerings to gods and ancestors;
the *prāgvaṃśa* hall is his body, he is radiant, and he is adorned with various initiations (*dīkṣā*). || 125 ||
The yogi is the southern fire-altar, the all-pervading lord consisting of the great sacrificial session;
he is adorned with the beautiful Upākarma and Iṣṭi rites as his whirlpools and the Pravargya ceremony as his ornaments. || 126 ||
With various inclinations and various paths of inclination, possessing secret esoteric teachings as his seat, he indeed stands like a lofty mountain peak together with his consort Chāyā. || 127 ||
Having become the Sacrificial Boar, that Lord, the Progenitor of Creatures, quickly entered the waters which had completely covered the earth. || 13 ||
Having approached her, he lifted her up and set her down;
he placed those waters from the ocean into the oceans and those from the rivers into the rivers.
For the sake of the welfare of the world, the Lord raised up with his tusk the earth, which had sunk into the depths of the netherworld and gone down to the subterranean realm.
Then, having brought the earth to its own place, that upholder of the earth, the supporter of the world, released it after having held it as before. || 16 ||
Above that flood of water, she stands like a great ship;
and because her body is so vast, the earth does not undergo submersion.
Then, having lifted up the earth with the desire to establish the world, the lotus-eyed Lord set his mind upon the division of the earth. || 18 ||
Having leveled the earth, he then piled up mountains upon it,
while the world was being consumed by the Saṃvartaka fire at the time of the previous dissolution.
By that fire, those mountains were completely shattered on the earth;
then, due to the coldness in that single ocean, the waters were withdrawn by the wind.
Wherever they were poured down, there they became immovable.
Because of that immovability they are called "acalas" (mountains), and because of their joints (*parvan*) they are known as "parvatas" (mountains). || 21 ||
Because they were swallowed by the waters and because they were piled up, the mountains are called *śiloccaya*s (heaps of rocks).
Then, when those world-ocean mountains had been scattered about, [the following occurred].
Viśvakarman divides this earth—along with its oceans, its seven continents, and its mountains—again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas. || 23 ||
Then he further fashioned the four worlds beginning with Bhūḥ;
and having fashioned the worlds, he indeed brought forth the creation of living beings. || 24 ||
The blessed Lord Brahmā, the self-existent, desiring to emit various creatures,
created an emission of that same nature as in former ages at the beginnings of the kalpas.
As he was then meditating upon creation with conscious intent, beings consisting of darkness (tamas) appeared simultaneously with the primary matter (pradhāna). || 26 ||
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and andhasaṃjñita—this fivefold ignorance has manifested, O Great-souled One. || 27 ||
The creation consisting of those possessed of self-conceit (abhimānin) exists in five states for one who meditates;
it is entirely enveloped by darkness, like a jar containing seeds. || 28 ||
Without light both externally and internally, they are indeed motionless and devoid of consciousness;
because their intellect is enveloped, their faculties [experience] only sufferings. || 29 ||
Therefore, those mountains are proclaimed to be the foremost among those whose natures are restrained.
Indeed, having seen that primary creation to be thus ineffective, Brahmā [reflected].
Then, with a mind that was not serene, he thought of something else; and as he was thus coveting, the downward stream (tiryak-srotas) turned toward him. || 31 ||
Because they have proceeded horizontally, they are known as *tiryaksrotas* (those with horizontal currents);
these are renowned as animals and the like, for they are all considered to abound in darkness (*tamas*) and to be full of ignorance.
The twice-born who follow a wrong path, and those who, while following a wrong path,
consider themselves wise in knowledge.
But having seen the second universe, the Lord indeed [created] those who flow horizontally;
possessed of egoism and self-conceit, they consist of twenty-eight kinds. || 321 ||

The elevenfold division of the faculties, as well as the ninefold arousal [of the winds], and the eight [winds] beginning with *tāraka*—these are recorded as the various modes of their power. || 322 ||
All of them are internally luminous but externally obscured;
because they proceed horizontally, they are called "horizontal-streamers" (tiryaksrotas). || 323 ||
But the Lord, having indeed seen the second universe flowing horizontally, and having perceived the arisen intention as well as such a creation, [proceeded]. || 324 ||
As he was meditating upon another, the Sāttvika beings indeed came into existence;
the third, however, was the Ūrdhvasrotas, who is established in the upward direction. || 33 ||
Because they turn away from there toward the upper realms, they are therefore known as "those who flow upward" (ūrdhvasrotas).
They abound in happiness and joy, and are restrained both externally and internally. || 34 ||
Those who are luminous both externally and internally are known as those born of the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas).

Through their union with *sattva*, those nine practitioners of alchemy (*dhātuvādins*) are indeed remembered as being born of *sattva*. Those wise ones are remembered as being contented in soul. || 35 ||
The three [classes] who flow upwards are indeed known as the divine creation (devasarga).
When those gods who flow upwards had been created, that Lord [then acted]. (36)
Brahmā became filled with joy; then he resolved upon another [creation]. That Lord, the Sovereign, created another creation that was effective for its purpose. || 37 ||
Then, as he was meditating with true meditation, there appeared from the unmanifest a practitioner who flowed downwards. || 38 ||

Because they turned back toward the lower [direction], they are therefore called *arvāk-srotas* (downward-streaming). They abound in light, yet are mixed with darkness and dominated by passion (*rajas*). || 39 ||
Therefore, those who repeatedly perform [actions] experience abundant suffering;
such men are manifest both outwardly and inwardly, and they are the ones who bring about [the results]. || 40 ||

By their characteristics, such as the stars and so forth, they are established in eight classes; these humans are perfected beings (siddhātman) who possess qualities similar to those of the Gandharvas. || 41 ||
Thus has been proclaimed this fiery creation, which flows downwards;
the fifth is the creation of grace, which is established in four ways. || 42 ||
Furthermore, through error, power, contentment, and likewise through perfection, they indeed know that object as both ceased and present. || 43 ||
That is called the sixth creation, consisting of beings such as the Bhūtas;
they were all possessors of property and again delighted in sharing.
They should be known as the devourers, the non-stones, and those consisting of the elements and so forth;
by way of inversion, the element-source (bhūtādi) is established through incapacity. || 45 ||
The first creation is that of the Mahat, which is to be known as belonging to Brahmā;
the second, however, is the creation of the subtle elements (tanmātras), which is called the creation of the gross elements (bhūtasarga). || 46 ||
But the third creation is that of Vaikārika, known as the creation of the senses;
thus this is the Prākṛta creation, which has arisen preceded by intelligence. || 47 ||
The fourth is the primary creation (mukhya-sarga), for the immobile beings are indeed known as the primary;
and that creation which flows horizontally is the fifth, consisting of those born of animal wombs (tairyagyonya). || 48 ||
Likewise, the sixth is that of those who flow upwards, which is known as the creation of the gods;
thereafter follows the seventh creation, that of those who flow downwards, which is the human creation. || 49 ||
The eighth is the creation of grace, which is both characterized by goodness (sāttvika) and darkness (tāmasa).
These five are the secondary creations (vaikṛta-sarga), while three are recorded as the primary creations (prākṛta-sarga). || 50 ||
The Prākṛta, the Vaikṛta, and the Kaumāra is recorded as the ninth.
The first three creations are considered Prākṛta; they were produced without prior conscious intent. || 51 ||
Those six creations of Brahmā proceed from his deliberate intention.
Now, listen as the creation of expansion and grace is being proclaimed! || 52 ||
Then he abides in all beings in their entirety in four ways:
through error, through power, through contentment, and likewise through perfection. || 53 ||
In stationary beings there is perversion; among those born as animals there is powerlessness; human beings are perfected souls; and among the gods there is complete satisfaction. || 53 ||
Thus, these nine are recorded as being both natural (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta);
they are also considered by the wise to be mutually affectionate and [bound] by causes. || 54 ||
In the beginning, Brahmā indeed created from his own mind seven beings equal to himself:
Sanandana, Sanaka, the wise Sanātana, and [the others]. || 55 ||

Those of great power have desisted through consciousness; by means of reversal, those of great splendor have turned back; and all three of them have likewise desisted from manifoldness upon becoming perfectly awakened. || 56 ||
Without having brought about the creation of progeny, they returned once more to the state of dissolution;
then, when those had passed away, [he created] other sons who were seekers of perfection.
Brahmā then created from his mind those presiding deities of the worlds,
by whom this earth is supported until the dissolution of all beings. || 58 ||

Śloka 5, Kāṇḍa 18–21: 18. Just as a man who has lost his way in a forest does not find the path even though he sees it, so too one who is deluded by ignorance does not perceive the Self, even though it is ever-present. 19. As a lamp placed inside a jar illuminates the interior but not the exterior, so the intellect, though it perceives objects, does not perceive that which is beyond itself. 20. As the sun, though it shines, is not seen by those whose eyes are closed, so the Self, though it is manifest, is not perceived by those whose minds are clouded by ignorance. 21. As a mirror, though it reflects forms, cannot reveal its own nature, so the mind, though it perceives all things, does not know the Self which is its own witness.
As well as the oceans and rivers, and likewise the mountains and forest trees. || 59 ||
Likewise, he is the self of the medicinal herbs, the self of trees and creepers, as well as the lava, kāṣṭhā, kalā, muhūrta, the junctions, and day and night. || 60 ||
Having first created the half-months, months, solstices, years, and yugas from his own body, he then created others:
both the gods and the ancestors, by whom these progeny were nourished. || 61 ||
He created nine mind-born sons: Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha. || 62 ||
"These nine Brahmās are established as such in the Purāṇas;
indeed, they are all of the nature of Brahman and are exponents of Brahman. (63)
Then Brahmā again created Rudra, who was born from his own wrath,
as well as Saṃkalpa and Dharma— the progenitor even of those who came before.
Then the Grandfather of all the worlds produced resolve, which brings happiness to all beings, and from that resolve he brought forth Dharma itself. || 65 ||
From his breath Brahmā created Dakṣa, and from his two eyes Marīci;
Bhṛgu was born from his heart, as was the sage Atri, who was born from the waters. || 66 ||
From his head he created Aṅgiras, and from his ear he likewise created Atri;
from his udāna breath he created Pulastya, and from his vyāna breath, furthermore, Pulaha.
From Samāna he created Vasiṣṭha, and from Apāna he fashioned Kratu;
these are remembered as the twelve divine sons of Brahmā. || 68 ||
Dharma and the others who were born first should be known as the sons of Brahmā;
however, those nine beginning with Bhṛgu, who were created later, are the exponents of Brahman.
They are the ancient householders; by them the Dharma was fully set forth.
These twelve, together with Rudra, indeed procreate offspring. || 70 ||
Both Ṛbhu and Sanatkumāra are those whose vital energy is drawn upward; for these two were born in the beginning, indeed the first-born of all. || 71 ||
They know that very [reality] as threefold, distinct yet undivided;
it is thus, and not thus, neither both nor neither. || 7412 ||
Those established in being and possessing equal vision declare that karma has its own specific object:
namely, the names of the self and the five elements, as well as their various elaborations. (7413)

By means of the word "Veda," that Great Lord fashioned these five [classes], as well as the names of the seers and whatever creations exist among the gods; at the end of the night, they are brought forth, and the Lord bestowed them once again upon those [beings]. || 7414 ||

Thus, this creation of the world arose from the Self-Existent Cause. The transformations beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa) are themselves derived from Prakṛti. || 7415 ||
The world, adorned with the sun and moon and graced by the constellations of planets,
is filled with rivers, oceans, and thousands of mountains.
In this forest of Brahman, filled with various delightful cities and prosperous provinces, the omniscient, unmanifested Brahmā moves about. || 7417 ||
Having its origin in the seed of the Unmanifest, it stands supported by that very [Unmanifest];
it consists of the trunk of the intellect and has the sense organs as its hollow interior. (7418)
It has the great elements as its branches and is possessed of leaves by way of particularities;
it has dharma and adharma as its beautiful flowers, and the arising of pleasure and pain as its fruit.
The eternal Brahma-tree is the livelihood of all beings;
it is indeed the forest of Brahman belonging to that very tree of Brahman.
That which is the unmanifest cause is eternal, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent;
it is what the investigators of reality call Pradhāna and Prakṛti.
Thus, this is known as the "gracious" creation (*anugraha-sarga*), which is occasional (*naimittika*) for Brahmā.
There are three other creations of Brahmā that are primordial (*prākṛta*) and not preceded by conscious intent (*abuddhipūrvaka*). || 7422 ||

But the six creations beginning with the primary one (mukhya) are modifications (vaikṛta), preceded by intelligence; they proceed from Brahmā through his volition and are characterized by his self-identification [with them]. || 7423 ||

Thus, these nine creations—both primary (prakṛta) and secondary (vaikṛta)—are recorded as being produced from one another; however, the wise consider [the primordial source] to be their ultimate cause. || 7424 ||
Know Him whose primordial source the Vedas proclaim as heaven, whose navel is the sky, whose eyes are the moon and sun,
whose ears are the quarters, and whose feet are the earth.
Thus, he is the inconceivable self, the leader of all beings. || 7425 ||
From whose mouth the Brahmins were born,
from the front part of whose chest the Kṣatriyas,
from whose thighs the Vaiśyas, and from whose feet the Śūdras.
All the social classes were produced from his limbs. || 7426 ||
Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest; the cosmic egg is born from the unmanifest.
From the egg, Brahmā was again born; by him the worlds were created himself. || 7427 ||

7.1–80) Thus has this first quarter, concerning the process of creation, been proclaimed. Having heard it, Kāpeya, with a delighted mind, asked about his doubts: 1. "Thus has this first quarter, concerning the process of creation, been proclaimed. Having heard it, Kāpeya, with a delighted mind, asks [his] questions."
Having gratified Sūta with his words, he then asked for the subsequent narrative:
"O knower of the Kalpas, from this point forward, please describe to us the reconnection [of the world]. || 2 ||
We wish to know, exactly as it is, the interval between this past eon and the present one, as well as the reconnection between these two; for you are indeed skilled! || 3 ||
Thus addressed by Kāpeya, Sūta, the best among speakers, began to relate the entire origin of the three worlds. (4)
Sūta said:
O you of excellent vows, I shall describe to you here, exactly as it is, the past and future Kalpas, as well as the period of transition between them. || 5 ||
O you of virtuous vows, those *manvantaras* which occurred during the various *kalpas*, and this auspicious *kalpa* currently proceeding, known as the Vārāha—[all these have been described]. || 6 ||
Now, learn of the state between this present kalpa and that eternal kalpa which preceded it and has passed away! || 7 ||
When the previous kalpa has been withdrawn, O sinless ones, another kalpa proceeds again and again from the world of living beings, without any further rebirth.
But for one whose rebirth-linking has been severed, there is an interval of an eon from eon to another;
at that time, at the end of the eon, all beings are completely annihilated in every way. || 9 ||
However, there is no reconnection between one kalpa and the next;
rather, the successions of the ages (yugas) within a Manvantara remain uninterrupted. || 10 ||
These proceed in succession with the Manvantaras and the Yugas;
those previous Kalpas have been described briefly for the sake of the systematic exposition. || 11 ||
Of those parārdha kalpas, that which was previously beyond this [present] parārdha is indeed the kalpa that has passed; it was a parārdha, but not the subsequent one. || 12 ||
O twice-born ones, there will be other kalpas which are doubled by the number of the latter half; among them, O brahmins, this present kalpa is the first, and it is now proceeding. || 13 ||
In this first half, however, the second is called "the beyond" (para);
such is the duration of the maintenance [of the world], and thereafter the withdrawal is traditionally taught. || 14 ||
But that eternal kalpa which preceded this present kalpa,
having occurred in the past at the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, together with its periods of Manvantaras— || 15 ||
When that eon was exhausted and the time of its conflagration had arrived,
those gods who were inhabitants of celestial palaces at that time in that eon— || 16 ||
The constellations, planets, and stars, as well as the moon, the sun, and so forth—
these indeed number twenty-eight times ten million for those of virtuous nature.
Just as in one Manvantara, so indeed in all fourteen;
there were three hundred and ninety-two crores [of verses]. (18)
Formerly, it is recorded that there were seventy-eight thousand [Vaimānika gods] who existed when the eon had passed. (19)
In each and every Kalpa, indeed, the gods residing in celestial chariots (Vaimānikas) are recorded;
furthermore, they have existed in heaven throughout the fourteen Manvantaras.
The gods and the ancestors, as well as the seers and the Manus, and those who are their followers, and likewise the sons of Manu. || 21 ||

And those gods who were worthy of worship by the members of the castes and stages of life at that time—those dwellers of heaven who existed in the various Manvantaras in the world of the gods. || 22 ||
Then, when the time of dissolution arrived, all of them, having attained equal perfection, reached union with those who had already attained such union at the onset of the universal deluge. || 23 ||
Then, because it was inevitable, those gods dwelling in the three worlds who preside over their respective stations here realized their own impending end. || 24 ||
When the *tāla* is thus complete and the final interval is near, the gods who dwell at the end of the eon [appear] when that calamity has arrived. (25)
Then, out of longing and despair, having abandoned their abodes with heartfelt devotion, they, being deeply agitated, set their minds upon Maharloka.
Endowed with these, they are reborn with bodies that abide in great splendor;
all of them, possessing abundant purity, have attained mental perfection. || 27 ||
Then a great assembly was convened together with those inhabitants of the Kalpa,
as well as with Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and other people born therein.
Having gone to Maharloka, those fourteen hosts of gods then set their minds, filled with anxiety, upon Janaloka. || 29 ||
All were abundant in purity and established in mental accomplishment;
they had attained [this state] together with those inhabitants of the Kalpa. || 30 ||
Having returned from there as if ten times, they go to their own austerity;
staying there for ten kalpas, they indeed go again to Satyaloka. || 31 ||
By this sequential process, those inhabitants of the eon passed away one after another;
thus, thousands of divine ages passed in succession.
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, they indeed attain a state from which there is no return; though lacking sovereign lordship, they are equal to him in their divine power. || 33 ||
They become equal to Brahmā in form and in their sphere of experience;
there they remain, endowed with joy and practicing self-restraint. || 34 ||
Having attained the bliss of Brahman, they are liberated along with Brahman;
by the very nature of things, through that which is inevitable, they [attain it] themselves. || 35 ||
Bound together by diversity, they exist at that particular time;
for just as one who is sleeping attains awakening preceded by consciousness, so it is indeed. || 36 ||
At that time, their knowledge proceeds in such a manner;
for those whose various powerful [faculties] have been differentiated by means of the withdrawals (pratyāhāra). || 37 ||
Together with them, they entrust their duties and instruments;
for those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā who perceive diversity. || 38 ||
For those whose offices have ceased and who abide in their own true nature, they are perfected ones of equal characteristics, pure in soul and stainless. (39)
Endowed with their instruments in the primordial state (prakṛti), they remain established in their own selves; having manifested themselves, primordial matter (prakṛti) truly exists within them.
The cognition [of them] as being other than the Puruṣa does not arise;
however, once creation has begun again, there is the cognition of those [beings] whose nature is accompanied by causes. || 41 ||
In the state of union (saṃyoga), the primordial nature (prakṛti) is to be known by those who are disciplined and perceive reality;
therein, for those who have attained liberation and shall not again enter the path of worldly existence. || 42 ||
Furthermore, their non-existence upon re-arising is like that of extinguished flames;
then, when those great-souled ones had departed from the three worlds, [the world was left behind]. (43)
Together with these, Maharloka was indeed not reached at that time;
those remaining here remain when the conflagration of the kalpa has arrived.
Those beginning with the Gandharvas and ending with the Piśācas, humans such as Brāhmaṇas and others, beasts, birds, and indeed stationary beings along with reptiles. || 45 ||
While those inhabitants of the earth's surface were present at that time,
that thousandfold radiance of the sun which shines here— || 46 ||
Having become those seven rays, each one arises as a sun;
rising up in succession, they utterly consume the three worlds.
The rivers, all the mountains,
and indeed all mobile and immobile beings were previously dried up by the lack of rain and scorched by those suns.
Then all of them, both mobile and immobile beings, consisting of merit and demerit, were rendered helpless and utterly consumed by the rays of the sun. || 49 ||
Then, at the end of the Yuga, their bodies having been consumed and their sins shaken off, they were indeed liberated from that fame which was bound up with both merit and demerit. || 50 ||
Then those people are indeed reborn among people of similar form;
all of them abound in purity and are established in mental accomplishment. || 51 ||
Having dwelt there for a night with Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
they become the mind-born offspring of Brahmā here again at the time of creation.
Then, when those inhabitants of the three worlds had descended and the worlds had been consumed by the seven suns, (53)
When the earth was flooded by rain and the oceans were devoid of water,
he [was] both the seals and the clouds, and all the waters belonging to the earth.
For those things called waters that depend upon it then attain the state of a single ocean;
and when there is a great volume of water characterized by coming and going, || 55 ||
Having completely covered this earth, it then became known as the ocean (arṇava);
for it shines with its own radiance, since the word *bhā* denotes both pervasion and light. || 56 ||
Having flooded everything on all sides, their water becomes manifest; it is called "water" (ambhas) because it extends throughout the entire earth in every direction. || 57 ||
The root *dhātu* means "to extend" or "to spread"; therefore, water (*ambhas*) is known as *tanavaḥ*.
The word *śara* refers to "shattered," while *aram* means "swiftly"; thus, the root is said to have various meanings. It is recorded by poets as a *nipāta* (an indeclinable particle). || 58 ||
The waters become a single ocean and do not flow swiftly; therefore, those men [remain there] when the day of Brahmā has come to an end after a thousand yugas. (59)
While that night was still proceeding, he remained in the form of water;
then, when that fire had vanished from the surface of the earth into the water, [he continued].
In a windless darkness where there was no light on any side, that very person who presided over this [world] was Brahmā, the Lord. || 61 ||
He then desired to effect the division of this world,
at that time when it had become a single ocean and all things mobile and immobile had perished.
Then he becomes that Brahmā, the thousand-eyed, the thousand-footed, the thousand-headed Puruṣa, golden-hued and indeed beyond the senses. || 63 ||
Then Brahmā, known as Nārāyaṇa, slept upon the waters;
awakened by the predominance of the quality of goodness (sattva), he beheld the world as a void.
And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa:
"We have heard that the name of the waters is 'nārāḥ' because their bodies are called 'nara';
since he dwells there having filled his navel with them, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (65)
The vital breaths indeed depart; [as it is said:

"Decaying, he who is called Puruṣa is Prajāpati, consisting of the three Vedas, possessing a thousand heads, a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, faces, and enjoyments, with a thousand arms, foremost. || 66 ||
Resplendent as the sun, the protector of the world, truly unique and without predecessor, the first to overcome the swift;
he is indeed recited as the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha), the Great-Souled Puruṣa, who stands beyond darkness. || 67 ||
At the beginning of the kalpa, becoming Brahmā with an abundance of rajas, he created all beings;
at the end of the kalpa, becoming Time with an abundance of tamas, he again devoured them.
He who is indeed called Nārāyaṇa, overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva), while sleeping upon the ocean, divides himself threefold and proceeds throughout the three worlds. || 69 ||
He himself creates, devours, and likewise withdraws by means of these three;
at that time, when the world has become a single ocean and all things mobile and immobile have perished.
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, when everything was enveloped by water,
Brahmā, known as Nārāyaṇa, was sleeping in the unmanifest ocean.
Having swallowed the fourfold classes of beings during the Brahma-night, the great seers behold him as Time sleeping in the great ocean from Maharloka.

At that time, there were the great seers Bhṛgu and others as previously mentioned; likewise, when the kalpa had passed, there were eight great seers beginning with Satya. Then, by those who were evolving, the supreme Great One was encompassed. || 73 ||
The derivation of the name is said to come from the verbal root *ṛṣ*, meaning "to go. Because they move among beings with great [power], they are therefore called Great Sages (*maharṣi*). || 74 ||
Then Kāla was seen by those residing in Maharloka while he was asleep;
they were the seven great sages who had existed in the kalpa that had passed, beginning with Satya.
Thus, after thousands of such Brahma-nights had passed, other great seers likewise beheld Time asleep. || 76 ||
Because Brahmā indeed fashioned the fourteen worlds many times at the beginning of a kalpa, it is therefore defined as a "kalpa. || 77 ||
He is the creator of all beings again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas;
he is Mahādeva, both manifest and unmanifest, and this entire world belongs to him. || 78 ||
Thus has this reconnection of the two Kalpas been described to you—the state that existed previously in the interval between the present and the past. || 79 ||
This has indeed been proclaimed in brief, exactly as it was, in a previous kalpa;
now I shall fully expound this kalpa—listen to it! || 80 ||

Primary Creation and Secondary Creation** At the end of the night, he assumes the state of Brahmā for the purpose of creation. (I. 7.1)
But Brahmā, having become the wind, was then moving within that water, while that ocean of darkness existed and all things mobile and immobile had perished. || 2 ||
When the surface of the earth was completely pervaded by water on all sides,
and when all beings had become indistinguishable and remained as mere existence, || 3 ||
Then the Lord, having lifted her up from within the waters, [placed] that earth... || 12 ||
Having established them in their own places, he further divided them;

Just as many mountains are situated at the end of the dissolution, so too were they established at the beginning of creation by their very nature and not otherwise. || 15 ||
The seven continents and the oceans are situated by their very nature in concentric circles around one another, each encircling the next. || 16 ||

And at the beginning of this kalpa, Brahmā indeed created the inhabitants:

The lavas, kāṣṭhas, and kalās, as well as the muhūrtas, the twilights, the nights, and the days; the half-months and the months, and the solstices, years, and yugas. (20)
Having created the various abodes and those who take pride in their respective stations,

at the beginning of the Kalpa, during the first age, the Kṛta-yuga, he first brought forth living beings.
Those beings whom I previously described to you in a former kalpa were, at the time that kalpa was dissolving, consumed by fire. || 23 ||
Those who have not reached the world of austerity (tapas) but have taken refuge in the world of men (jana), they indeed persist and become seeds for the sake of creation once again. || 24 ||
They remained there for the sake of the seed, again as the cause of creation;
then, being created, they indeed exist for the sake of continuity.
It is traditionally held that these [sciences] are established here for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
likewise, they belong to the gods, the ancestors, the seers, and human beings. 26.
Then, endowed with ascetic power, they indeed fill those stations;
for they become the perfected souls who are the mind-born sons of Brahmā. || 27 ||
Through actions joined with attachment and aversion, they have gone to heaven;
returning here, they are born again age after age. || 28 ||
Through the remnants of the fruits of their own karma, they become known as being of that very nature;
they arise from the world of people due to the bondage of doubt regarding karma. || 29 ||
One should understand that intention (*āśaya*) is the cause of those actions;
indeed, by means of those auspicious and inauspicious actions, beings are born from the world of men (*janaloka*). || 30 ||
They take up bodies of various forms within the wombs; from the gods down to the stationary beings, they are born one after another. || 31 ||
Whatever actions they performed prior to creation, those very same actions they undertake again and again as they are being created. || 32 ||

Violent and non-violent, gentle and cruel, righteous and unrighteous, true and false—impregnated by these, they enter [into new births]; therefore, that which is habitual to them is what pleases them. || 33 ||
Whatever names of forms existed throughout the eons that have passed, those very same ones were for the most part adopted in the future time as well. || 34 ||
Therefore, those very things attained the state of name-and-form;
again and again in successive kalpas, they are born as name-and-form entities.
Then, indeed, when the creation was firmly established for Brahmā who desired to emit [the world], || 35 ||
Krauṣṭuki said:
You have described the downward-flowing stream that pertains to human beings;
O Brahmin, tell me in detail how Brahmā created it. || 35 ||
O Mahāmati, tell me how he created the castes and what their qualities were, and what the traditional duties of the Brahmins and the others are said to be! || 35 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "In the beginning, as Brahmā was creating while contemplating with truth,"
As he was then meditating upon those progeny with true intent,
he indeed created a thousand pairs from his mouth. || 36 ||
For those people were born endowed with the quality of purity (sattva), possessed of great splendor;
he then created another thousand pairs from his chest. || 37 ||
All of them were dominated by passion (rajas), full of vigor, and impatient;
he then created another thousand from his thighs who were likewise ill-disposed. || 38 ||
Those who were predominant in rajas and tamas are remembered as being of a striving nature.
He then created another thousand pairs from his two feet. || 39 ||
Overwhelmed by darkness, they were all devoid of splendor and possessed little luster;
then those living beings, born of pairs, began to rejoice.
Overcome by mutual desire, they proceeded to engage in sexual union.
From that time forward in this kalpa, the origin of procreation through pairs is said to have occurred. || 41 ||
Whatever monthly menstrual flow women normally have occurred, that indeed ceased for them;
therefore, at that time, they did not give birth even though sexual intercourse was practiced. || 42 ||
At the end of their lifespan, those *kuṭakas* and *kuvikas*, desiring to die, give birth only once to twins;
having produced a family from whence, they then abandoned their bodies. (43)
From that time forward, in this kalpa, the birth of pairs indeed occurs; for those beings, offspring are produced repeatedly through meditation and the mind alone. || 44 ||
The pure objects of sense, beginning with sound, each possess five characteristics; such was this human creation that formerly belonged to Prajāpati. || 45 ||
Born in his lineage, they have filled this world;
they frequent rivers, lakes, and oceans, as well as mountains. || 46 ||
Then, indeed, those [beings] move about in that Yuga with little hunger, cold, or heat;
they consume food known as the "essence of the earth."
Those creatures, moving according to their will, resorted to mental perfection. || 47 ||
O Mahāmati, they have attained natural satisfaction regarding sense objects. || 47 ||
In those [beings] of the Kṛta Yuga at the beginning of the aeon, neither merit nor demerit existed; those creatures were without distinction. Their lifespan, happiness, and form were equal.
In those [beings] of the Kṛta Yuga at the beginning of the aeon, neither merit nor demerit existed. (47)
In the Kṛta Yuga, they were born according to their respective offices;

They say the first age is Kṛtayuga, along with its two junctions (saṃdhyā and saṃdhyāṃśa), each consisting of four hundred [years].
Then, even as those thousands of progeny became widely known... 47.
They experience no resistance, no duality, nor even any suffering;
for they dwell among mountains and oceans, having no fixed abode as their refuge. 48.

Piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas, as well as envious people, beasts,
and birds.
Crocodiles, fish, and reptiles— whether they are water-dwellers or egg-born— for these are indeed born of unrighteousness. || 50 ||
At that time, there were no beasts, nor birds, nor reptiles; there were no beings born from sprouts, nor any denizens of hell.

and so, during their forenoon, they—

Furthermore, for those who desired it in that way, satisfaction arose without effort;

From the subtlety of the waters, their accomplishment arose, shining with various flavors, and yet another [quality] was produced.

Whatever desires they mentally long for arise everywhere and at all times upon this earth.
Meditated upon by them, she arises from the essence;
her accomplishment brings strength and complexion, and she is the devourer of diseases. || 52 ||
Their bodies were unconditioned by effort, and those creatures possessed perpetual youth;
indeed, their offspring were born as pairs without any sexual union. || 53 ||
Their birth was equal, their form was equal, and they died together.
At that time, truth, freedom from greed, patience, contentment, happiness, and self-restraint were present;
for all of them were without distinction in terms of appearance, lifespan, conduct, and behavior. || 54 ||
The activity of living beings arises spontaneously, without being preceded by conscious intent. || 54 ||
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was no activity of either virtuous or sinful deeds; at that time, there were neither the established orders of castes and stages of life nor any intermixture of them.
Free from desire and aversion, they live together with one another;
all are equal in form and lifespan, devoid of the distinctions of inferior or superior. || 55 ||
In the Kṛtayuga, those who are happy and free from sorrow are born;

For them, gain and loss, friend and foe, and the pleasant and unpleasant do not exist; for those who have withdrawn [from the world], the object of the mind proceeds as one free from desire. || 552 ||
They do not harm one another, nor indeed do they show favor to one another.
Meditation is said to be supreme in the Kṛta age, while knowledge is said to be so in the Tretā age. || 553 ||

Sacrifice is prevalent in the Dvāpara age, while charity is best in the Kali age; goodness (sattva) belongs to the Kṛta age, passion (rajas) to the Tretā, and both passion and darkness (rajas-tamas) to the Dvāpara. || 554 ||
Kali is to be understood as darkness (tamas) according to the nature of the age-cycle;
this is the time in the Kṛta-yuga—learn its measurement! || 555 ||
The Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand divine years;
its two junctions (saṃdhyā and saṃdhyāṃśa) are eight hundred in number.
The lifespan of those women at that time was four thousand years of human reckoning.
And misfortunes do not arise from the afflictions. || 56 ||
And there are no afflictions or misfortunes. || 56 ||
Then, when that Kṛta Yuga had passed along with its transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśa),
the dharma of the age remained in its entirety as a mere quarter-remnant.
Even when the twilight has passed, it is the end of the Yuga;
however, when one quarter of the Yuga's twilight remains, [the world] is still left.
When this had been performed completely, spiritual power (siddhi) then vanished;
and when that mental power was lost,
another kind of power arose in the subsequent age called Tretā, following the Kṛta.

Those eight mental [perfections] which were indeed proclaimed by me at the beginning of creation—those eight perfections come to total destruction through the sequential application [of the path]. || 564 ||
At the beginning of the kalpa, this perfection indeed exists on Mount Mānasa;

The accomplishment of ritual action is said to arise from the conduct prescribed for one's caste and stage of life;
it is produced by a quarter of the twilight rite, and by a partial quarter of the twilight rite. || 566 ||
For these [ages] have their portions of prosperity already spent; the qualities of the ages—asceticism, sacred learning, strength, and lifespan—each diminish by one-third in succession. || 567 ||
Then, O best of sages, when the portion of Kṛta had been exhausted, the emergence of the Tretā Yuga followed, along with its own specific portion. || 568 ||
Furthermore, at various places, the earth was once possessed of all prosperity through good fortune,

Just as living beings approach [their end]. || 57 ||
In that manner, those [powers], having been perfected everywhere, gradually went to destruction;

Men descended from the sky;

When that [period] has been exhausted and its portion completed, among the remaining subjects here at the commencement of the kalpa...
Then, at the beginning of the Tretā age.
Then, through the conjunction of time, success perishes; it is not otherwise.
