Another accomplishment was born. || 571 ||
When the subtlety of the waters has then returned to the nature of clouds, from those clouds accompanied by thunder...
The release of rain has begun. || 572 ||
When the surface of the earth was thus moistened by that single rain,
their [seeds] then appeared.
But trees are designated as "houses. || 58 ||
But all their enjoyment arises from those [objects];
at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, living beings subsisted upon them. || 59 ||
Then, in the course of time, there occurred in them a sudden passion due to the monthly arising of their menses.
Furthermore, there is the repeated arising in a womb. || 60 ||
Then, through the arising of passion for them, those trees came to be designated as "houses. || 61 ||
O Brahmin, moreover, the branches of other great trees fell down,
and garments as well as ornaments were produced from their fruits. || 62 ||
In those very places, within each and every leaf-cup, there arises honey endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor; it is not produced by bees and possesses great potency. || 63 ||
By means of that, they indeed subsisted during the mouth of the Tretā Yuga;
through that accomplishment, the subjects were joyful, contented, and free from all affliction.
Then, after some time had passed, those women, again overcome by greed and their minds possessed by the sense of "mine," took possession of the trees. || 65 ||
Due to that transgression, even those trees perished for them;
thereafter, couples were born.
Indeed, cold, heat, hunger, and so forth. || 66 ||
In order to destroy those bonds,
they first constructed cities;
they then surrounded themselves with trees.
Or honey from bees [is extracted] by force. || 65 ||
Due to that misconduct of theirs, brought about once again by greed,
they were utterly destroyed along with the honey.
In various places, there were wish-fulfilling trees. || 65 ||
When that very accomplishment had become diminished due to the power of time,
then their [practices] began to prevail.
But the pairs of opposites have arisen. || 66 ||
Then, due to intense cold, wind, and heat, they were greatly afflicted;
being tormented by these pairs of opposites, they suffered intensely.
And they created protective enclosures. || 66 ||
Having provided remedies for the pairs of opposites,
they indeed took refuge in dwellings;
for previously, they had moved about according to their own will.
They lived without taking recourse to a fixed abode. || 66 ||
In former times, they dwelt in their dwellings according to their needs and according to their pleasure—
in desert wastes, in lowlands, on mountains, and by rivers.
And they take refuge in fortresses— whether in trees, on mountains, or in water—
as well as in artificial fortresses, measuring them out with their own fingers.
The means of valid cognition were previously established for the purpose of defining measurement;
the atom (paramāṇu) is the ultimate subtle [unit].
A *trasareṇu* is a particle of dust from the earth. || 69 ||
A hair-tip, a nit, a louse-egg, and the interior of a barley grain—
each of these is eleven times the size of the preceding one.
Likewise, the finger-breadth (aṅgula) has a barley-corn in its middle. || 70 ||
A foot is six finger-breadths, and two spans (vitasti) make one cubit (sinṛta);
these are to be applied according to what is appropriate and as desired.
On even ground and on uneven ground. || 66 ||
They indeed began to construct dwellings to ward off cold and heat;
then they built them.
And formerly there were villages and cities as well. || 68 ||
He likewise [assigned] the villages according to their respective shares, as well as the inner apartments; he [determined] their lengths and breadths.
And other types of arrangements. || 68 ||
Then, having measured again and again with their own fingers according to their wisdom,
they established the standard measures for the purpose of measurement.
From that time forward, they performed [these rites]. || 69 ||
A region of ten finger-joints is one barley-corn (yava); three of these are a cubit (hasta), a fathom (kiṣku), and a bow (dhanus).
It is designated by the name "prādeśa. || 70 ||
The span between the thumb and the forefinger is called a *prādeśa*; it is recorded that a *tāla* is measured by the middle finger.
And Gokarṇa was also afflicted with disease. || 71 ||
Two spans (vitasti) likewise constitute a cubit (hasta); this is the measurement for wrapping [the cloth] starting from the Brāhmya-tīrtha. || 71 ||
A span measured by the little finger is said to be twelve finger-breadths;
a ratni consists of finger-joints.
In terms of number, however, there are twenty-one. || 71 ||
Twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) shall constitute one cubit (hasta);
two cubits are traditionally known as one fathom (kiṣku).
It is forty-two finger-breadths [in length]. || 71 ||
A staff and a pair of arrows measure four cubits;
two thousand bows make one *gavyūti*, and four times that [makes a *yojana*]. || 72 ||
And this supreme *yojana* has been declared by the wise for the purpose of calculation. || 73 ||
There, two thousand bow-lengths are reckoned as one *gavyūti*. || 72 ||
Eight thousand bows are defined as one *yojana*;
by this very *yojana* [the following measurements are determined].
Then the settlement was established. || 73 ||
Now, of the four types of fortresses, three were self-originated;
the fourth was an artificial fortress, which they constructed with great effort. || 74 ||
O twice-born one, there are likewise Pura, Keṭaka, Droṇīmukha,
and Śākhānagaraka.
Likewise, the triple Veda [is located] at Karvaṭaka. || 74 ||
The arrangement of the village's sound and layout,
as well as separate dwellings within them;
the fourth is the artificial fort.
I shall explain the ritual procedure for that. || 74 ||
It was equipped with high ramparts and walls, and surrounded on all sides by moats. || 75 ||
Rucaka, Svastikadvāra, Kumārīpura, Srotasīsaṃhatadvāra, and Nikhāta once again. || 75 ||

Eight cubits and ten are considered the best for all types of villages—whether they consist of fields, ancient towns, or ordinary settlements; others, however, are held to be nine or eight [cubits]. || 752 ||
And [he should know] the extent of the width and length of the three kinds of fortresses—those consisting of mountains, water, and archers—as well as those that are artificial. || 753 ||
With a width of one-quarter of a yojana and a length of half of that eighth part,
it is praised when sloping toward the east and north,
and its bamboo framework extends outward from the pure [foundation]. || 76 ||
A *kheṭa* should be half that size, a *karvaṭa* a quarter of that,
and a *droṇīmukha* smaller than that.
And it is also expressed by means of its internal portion. || 77 ||
A city devoid of walls and moats is called "armored," as is another type known as a branch-city (śākhānagaraka).
Possessing ministers, vassals, and provincial territories. || 78 ||
Likewise, [a city] that consists mostly of Śūdras, whose prosperity depends on its own agriculture,
and which is situated amidst lands intended for cultivation, [is of a certain type].
A dwelling known as a village. || 79 ||
That dwelling which is constructed by men for some purpose other than [their own] city or the like, indeed—
The dwelling place should be known as being for those who are new. || 80 ||
One who is mostly wicked, who wanders through the lands of others without his own fields, and is powerful,
is known as a "village worm."
He relies upon the favor of the king's favorite. || 81 ||
With goods loaded onto carts and without a marketplace, there was likewise a herd of cows and a cowherd settlement.
Wherever there is desire, there is the banner of the stages. || 82 ||
Having thus created cities and so forth for their own dwelling, they made them into abodes for pairs [of opposites].
They indeed prepared dwellings for him. || 83 ||
Just as those trees had previously been in the shape of houses,
he recollected all of that exactly as it was.
Those subjects built houses.
Just so have the branches of this tree gone, and likewise others have gone;
they are both bent down and uplifted.
In the same way, they fashioned the branches. || 85 ||
O best of the twice-born, those very branches that formerly belonged to the wish-fulfilling trees have now become the branches of houses.
Therefore, the nature of a house exists in them by means of that [name]. || 86 ||
Beyond this, there are others who have gone upward,
and likewise others who have gone across;
having investigated these according to reason with one's intellect, [one should understand them].
Just as the branches of a tree have gone [downward], || 85 ||
Since they were made by them in that manner, those branches (śākhās) are therefore remembered as śālās;
thus they are well-known from the branches.
And likewise, halls and houses. || 86 ||
Therefore, those [deities] are remembered as "śālās," and the state of being a *śālā* resides within them;
for they are propitiated in them.
From that [wood], they were designated as palaces;
therefore, houses, halls, and palaces are so named. || 861 ||
Having suffered those mutual afflictions, they then reflected upon the means of livelihood,
for the wish-fulfilling trees had vanished along with the honey.
Those creatures, agitated by despair and afflicted by thirst and hunger, then experienced the manifestation of supernatural powers (siddhi) during that Tretā Yuga. 88.
There is yet another rain that accomplishes the purpose of livelihood; it is the abundance of those [clouds].
Whatever waters from their rain fall here into the lowlands, || 89 ||
By means of the rain, the lowlands became manifest, as did the channels, the excavations, and the rivers;
thus the rivers came into being during the second creation of rain. (90)
Those drops of water which had fallen from above onto the surface of the earth, through their union with the earth, then became medicinal herbs. || 91 ||
Then there were born medicinal herbs yielding flowers, roots, and fruits;
fourteen kinds in total, both cultivated and wild, which grow without being ploughed or sown. 92.
Trees and shrubs were produced that bore flowers and fruit according to the seasons; and in the Tretā age, the manifestation of medicinal herbs for the sake of livelihood occurred.
At that time, during the Tretā Yuga, living beings subsisted on medicinal herbs;
yet, having encountered passion and greed,
those beings then became subject to sudden calamities.
Those perfected souls who were previously described by me in the Kṛta age,
or those who have arisen here from Janaka as the mind-born sons of Brahmā— || 951 ||
Those who were peaceful as well as those who were vigorous, and likewise those who were active and suffering,
having proceeded from that state, were born again during the Tretā age.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise people of mixed castes, were all conditioned by their auspicious and inauspicious actions in their previous births. || 953 ||
But those among them who were strong in truth, non-violent, free from greed, and self-controlled, indeed continued to dwell there. || 954 ||
Others of lesser splendor do not take them as their own; those who are even weaker perform the tasks for them. || 955 ||
They engage in services for one another, while others possess little splendor;
thus they act with mutual opposition toward those who have approached [the path]. 956.
O twice-born one, because of that fault, those herbs perished even as people looked on;
the earth swallowed them all at once.
Then, O Mahāmati, there were medicinal herbs. || 96 ||
Then, when those [plants] had perished, those creatures, being bewildered and driven by hunger, went for refuge to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
And having understood in truth that the earth was being swallowed up at that time,
he made Sumeru his calf and milked this earth.
Then, by him, this cow was milked for seeds upon the surface of the earth. || 98 ||
Those seeds were born again as both cultivated and wild plants;
these medicinal herbs, which end with the ripening of their fruit, are recorded as seventeen groups. || 99 ||
Rice and barley, wheat and millet, sesame seeds, fine priyaṅgu grains, and indeed the noble koradūṣa and cīnaka beans. || 100 ||
Māṣas, mudgas, masūras, niṣpāvas, along with kulatthas, āḍhakīs, nakas, and śaṇas—these are recorded as the seventeen [grains]. || 101 ||
Thus, these are recorded as the species of cultivated plants; indeed, there are fourteen types of sacrificial plants, both cultivated and wild. 102.
Rice, barley, beans, wheat, millet, sesame, and *priyaṅgu* as the seventh—these are [the grains]; however, lentils (*kulatthikā*) are the eighth.
Now, śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila, gavedhuka,
kuruvinda, bamboo-grains (veṇuyava), and those which are markaṭaka—
these are remembered as the fourteen plants, both cultivated and wild. || 104 ||
For these plants first appeared at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga; they were all cultivated and wild herbs that did not require plowing with a furrow. || 104 ||
Trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and species of grasses, growing by their roots, fruits, and flowers, bore fruit without being cultivated. || 104 ||
The seeds which were formerly milked from the Earth by the Self-existent One indeed arose here as herbs, consisting of seasonal flowers and fruits. || 104 ||
When the plants, having been released, did not sprout again,
he then devised a means of livelihood for them by way of agriculture.
The blessed, self-existent Brahmā [bestowed] the accomplishment of success through the hands born of ritual action;
from that time forward, medicinal herbs grew as crops cultivated by plowing. || 106 ||
When the means of livelihood had been fully established, Prajāpati then fixed the boundaries for them according to what was right and according to their respective qualities. || 107 ||
Those who were indeed the possessors of those [women] were the most powerful;
he established the other Kṣatriyas as protectors who had performed their duties. || 107 ||
So many attend upon them as there are those who are fearless, and those Brahmins who speak the truth of Brahman exactly as it is. || 107 ||
And whatever other weaklings there were, established in cruel deeds, those usurers, previously untiring, brought about the destruction upon the earth. || 107 ||
They call those very ones Vaiśyas, the Kīnāśas who provide their livelihood;
they serve and run about, devoted to acts of attendance. || 107 ||
Devoid of splendor and possessing little vigor, he spoke to those Śūdras:
"O best among the upholders of dharma, [I shall explain] the duties of the social classes and the stages of life."
Once the fourfold order of society had indeed been established by him,
those subjects nevertheless failed, out of delusion, to observe those duties once again.
Living by means of the duties of the Vaiśyas, they obstructed one another.
But the Lord Brahmā, having understood that matter exactly as it was, [acted]. (108)
He ordained that for Kṣatriyas, their strength lies in punishment, warfare, and the profession of arms;
while for Brāhmaṇas, it consists of officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts. (108)
He assigned these duties to those powerful Brāhmaṇas;
he gave cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture to the Vaiśyas. || 108 ||
The Lord ordained the livelihood of crafts and service for the Śūdras;
however, he further assigned common duties to the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts are common to all of them;
having assigned these as their means of livelihood from among those [occupations], they may also give to one another.
For all the castes among the people who correctly protect dharma and artha,
the station of Prajāpati is ordained for those Brāhmaṇas who perform their ritual duties. || 109 ||
The station of Indra belongs to Kṣatriyas who do not flee in battles;
the station of Marut belongs to Vaiśyas who subsist by their own duty; the station of the Gandharvas belongs to those of the Śūdra caste who follow the practice of service. || 110 ||
"These are the stations for the social classes who abide in proper conduct;
therefore, once the classes were established, he established the stages of life. || 110 ||
The householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—the Lord established these four stages of life (āśramas) as before. || 110 ||

Those who do not perform any of the duties pertaining to their social class (varṇa) or stage of life (karma) in this world, those residing in the various stages of life (āśrama) declare that their performed actions have perished. || 110 ||
Brahmā established those [hermitages] according to their respective names;
then, for the purpose of instructing them, Brahmā proclaimed the dharmas.
Their various paths, as well as their restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), have been declared;
first of all, the stage of the householder is said to consist of the four castes.
I shall now explain, in due order, the foundation and the very source of the three stages of life, as well as their restraints and observances. || 110 ||
Wife, sacred fires, hospitality toward guests, sacrificial offerings, ancestral rites, and progeny—this, indeed, is the summary of the duties of a householder. || 110 ||
Carrying a staff, wearing a girdle, sleeping on the ground, and likewise having matted hair;
service to the teacher and living on alms are the duties of the student for the sake of sacred knowledge. || 110 ||

Rags, leaves, and skins shall be their clothing; forest roots, fruits, and medicinal herbs their food; and bathing at both twilights, as well as the fire-oblation, shall be the duties of those dwelling in the forest. || 110 ||
He further established for them places at the summit of the world-intervals;
and when the pestle had failed, he ordained alms-gathering, non-stealing, and purity.
Heedfulness, non-negligence, compassion for all beings, and patience. || 11010 ||
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, and truthfulness are recorded as the tenth;
for this Dharma consisting of ten characteristics was proclaimed by the Self-Existent One. Herein, there are five vows for a monk and likewise five secondary vows. || 11011 ||
Purity of conduct, discipline, cleanliness, non-attachment to worldly objects, and right view—these indeed are the five minor vows (upavrata). || 11012 ||
Meditation is the concentration of the mind and senses; having then approached for alms from those who possess the ocean-like [teachings],
liberation comes through silence and those purified by sacred observances.
The wandering mendicants proclaim this Dharma. || 11013 ||
All stages of life were proclaimed by Brahmā himself for the sake of ultimate welfare;
they consist of truth, uprightness, austerity, patience, yoga, sacrifice, and self-restraint as their foremost quality.
The Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, the sacrifices, the vows, and the observances—none of these succeed for one who is corrupted when a defect of disposition has arisen. || 11015 ||
All external rituals may sometimes succeed for one whose internal disposition is corrupted, even though he performs them with great effort. || 11016 ||
Even one who might give away all his possessions with a defiled inner self would not be a partaker of Dharma; for in this matter, the internal disposition alone is the cause.
In this way, the gods, along with the ancestors, the seers, and likewise the Manus—
their station for those who are established there in that world is proclaimed.
The abode that is prescribed for the sixty-four thousand sages who have drawn up their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) is the very same as that of those who dwell with their guru. || 111 ||
The station of the Seven Sages is indeed remembered as that of the forest-dwellers;
the station of Prajāpati is for householders, and the abode of Brahmā is for renunciants.
For yogis there is the immortal station, but it does not exist for those with various [worldly] thoughts.
These are the stations of those in the stages of life who are established in their own dharma;
these four paths leading to the gods have been fashioned. || 1121 ||

Those paths of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) are recorded as being exactly four, established by Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds, upon the earth during the first Manvantara. As for those paths of the gods (devayāna), the sun is recorded as their gateway. || 112 ||
In the same way, the moon is said to be the gateway for those who travel by the path of the ancestors.
Thus, when the divisions of the social classes and stages of life had been established at that time. || 112 ||
When his progeny, consisting of the various castes and stages of life, did not increase,
he then created other mental beings during the middle of the Tretā age.
But as for the self and the body, they are indeed equal to the self;
however, when that first Tretā Yuga had reached its middle stage, there was a gradual change.
Then he proceeded to create other mental offspring;
thereafter, the Lord created beings in whom the qualities of *sattva* and *rajas* were predominant. (112)
It is the means for accomplishing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as the livelihood (vārtā); likewise, it is the path for the gods, the ancestors, the seers, and the Manus. || 112 ||
By them, these subjects were increased in accordance with dharma and suited to the age;
then, when that class of created beings had appeared before the Self-born One.
He meditated upon all the mental progeny of various forms who had been previously mentioned by me to you as having taken refuge in Janaloka. || 112 ||
In a past aeon, those beings here were indeed gods and others;
as he meditated, they all appeared before him for the sake of procreation.
In the progression of the Manvantaras, those who were previously manifested here by those very ancestors are considered the youngest, yet they are renowned precisely through their lineages. || 112 ||
At that time, beings were for the most part characterized by wholesome and unwholesome actions;
supported by the remainder of the fruits of those actions, they continued to exist. || 112 ||
By the gods, asuras, and ancestors; by the yakṣas, gandharvas, and humans;
and by those rākṣasas and piśācas, as well as by beasts, birds, and reptiles. || 11213 ||
Appearing in various forms such as trees, hell-beings, and insects, he indeed fashioned these selves for the sake of providing support for all living beings. || 11214 ||
1. Section: Sarga and Pratisarga | Chapter 6 (Bḍ. I. 8.1–66; L. 70.195b–261a, 324b–344; Vā.
9.1–122) Then, as he was meditating, mental offspring were born to him, together with those effects and causes produced from his own body. || 1 ||
From the limbs of that wise one, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) came forth;
from them, the fourfold group—gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans—arose. || 2 ||
Desiring to emit these waters, he joined himself with his own self;
then, from him whose self was thus joined, there arose the manifestation of the constituent of darkness (tamas).
As the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) meditated upon that creation, an effort arose within him;
then, from his loins, the Asuras were first born as his sons. || 4 ||
The wise have remembered *asu* to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*); because they were born from that, they are called *asuras*.
He cast off that body by which all the *surās* were created. || 5 ||
That body, cast away by him, immediately became night;
because it was abounding in darkness (*tamas*), therefore night consists of three watches (*triyāmikā*). || 6 ||
Because creatures were enveloped by darkness at night, they therefore slept;
then, having created the Asuras, he assumed another body.
Then he directed that [energy], which was unmanifest and abounding in the quality of goodness (sattva);
as he was thus applying it, O Lord, it became truly dear to him. || 8 ||

Then, from the mouth of that one as he was playing, the deities were born. Because they were born while he was playing (*divyataḥ*), they are therefore celebrated as "Devas" (the Shining Ones). || 9 ||
The root which is declared to mean "to play" (div) is understood here as such;
therefore, from that divine body, the deities were born. || 10 ||
Then, having created the gods, the Lord of Gods assumed another body;
that body, once cast off by him, immediately became the day. || 11 ||
Therefore, on that day, the deities devoted themselves to ritual action.
Having created the gods, he then assumed another body; thereafter, he took on yet another body, consisting solely of the essence of *sattva*. || 12 ||
Thinking of them as his sons, the Lord meditated upon them;
for the Pitṛs were born from his two armpits during the interval between night and day. || 13 ||
Therefore, those ancestors are gods; by that [act], the state of being ancestors resides in them.
However, he cast off that body by which the ancestors had been created. || 14 ||
Casting off that body, she immediately became the twilight;
therefore, it is remembered that the day belongs to the gods and the night to the Asuras. || 15 ||
Of these three, that body which belongs to the ancestors is indeed the most important;
therefore, all the gods, asuras, sages, and likewise the Manus [worship it]. (16)
Being disciplined, they worship that middle body of Brahmā;
therefore, the twice-born likewise worship the junction of night and day.
Thereafter, Brahmā indeed assumed another body. || 17 ||
The Lord then created from his mind those whose nature consisted of the quality of rajas;
thereafter, from that state dominated by rajas, he created his mind-born sons. || 18 ||
From his mind, however, human beings were born as offspring; they are called "men" (manuṣya) because of their thinking (manana), and "offspring" (prajā) because of their procreation (prajana).
Having thus created offspring, he cast off that body of his. || 19 ||
Her body was pierced by him and immediately became moonlight;
therefore, living beings become filled with joy at the rising of the moon. || 20 ||
Thus, these bodies were cast off by that Great-Souled One;
immediately thereafter, night and day, as well as the twilight and the moonlight, came into being.

Moonlight, twilight, and likewise day—these three consist of the quality of goodness (sattva); night consists of the quality of darkness (tamas), and for that reason it indeed has three watches (triyāmikā). || 22 ||
Therefore, the gods were indeed created from the mouth by the Creator with satisfaction during the day;
since their birth was during the day, they are strong by day. || 23 ||
When the Lord, having struck down the Asuras with his body during the night, released them from their vital breaths, they were born of the night; therefore, they are unbearable at night. || 24 ||
These very same [elements] belong to the future gods along with the asuras,
and to the ancestors and humans, throughout both the past and the future.
Indeed, in all the Manvantaras, there are four causes:
moonlight, night, day, and twilight; these are the four waters.

Because they shine (*bhānti*), therefore they are "waters" (*ambhāṃsi*); this word *bhā* has been declared by the sages to signify both pervasion and radiance. Furthermore, then, Prajāpati... || 27 ||
Having created these waters, he then created the gods, dānavas, and humans, as well as the ancestors and various other beings from himself once again. || 28 ||
Having cast off that body of moonlight, the Lord then assumed another form, consisting primarily of *rajas* and *tamas*, and joined it once again. || 29 ||
Then the Lord created others who were hungry and afflicted by darkness;
those created by him, being of the nature of hunger, set about to seize the waters. || 30 ||
"We shall protect these waters," they said; those among them who spoke thus were therefore known as *rākṣasas*, the night-stalkers whose nature is hunger. || 31 ||
Those who said, "We shall exhaust the waters," rained upon one another;
by that deed, they became *yakṣas* and *guhyakas* of cruel actions. || 32 ||
This verbal root is understood to mean "to protect" (*pālana*); and that which is this root *kṣi*, is explained as meaning "to destroy" (*kṣapaṇa*).
[Because of protecting, he is called *rakṣa*; because of destroying, he is called *yakṣa*. || 33 ||
Indeed, upon seeing them, the hair of that wise woman fell out in distress; once fallen, it rose upward and then climbed back onto her head. || 34 ||
Because their hair has fallen from their heads and because they have slithered away, they are known as *vyāla*s; because they are base (*hīna*), they are known as *ahi*s. || 35 ||
They are called *pannagas* because they have fallen down (*pannatvāt*), and they are called *sarpas* because of their crawling away (*apasarpaṇāt*).
Their dwellings on the earth are below the sun and the moon. || 36 ||
That most terrible fire born of his wrath, which was of the nature of poison, entered the serpents who were born together with him. || 37 ||
Then, out of anger, having created serpents, he produced beings whose very nature was wrath;
tawny in color, they were fierce and devourers of flesh. 38.
From Bhūta came those known as the Bhūtas; from Piśita-āśana (the eater of flesh) came the Piśācas.
Then, from him while he was sucking the cow, the Gandharvas were born as his sons. || 39 ||
The root *dhā* is indeed taught in the sense of drinking;
those who were born drinking the Vāc are therefore remembered as Gandharvas. || 40 ||
When these eight classes of divine beings had been created, that Lord then, by his own will, produced other birds from his own vital energy. || 41 ||
Having created the beasts according to their own will, as well as the birds according to their own will, that Lord of Gods also created the flocks of winged creatures. || 42 ||
Then Brahmā emitted goats from his mouth; he created sheep from his chest, and he brought forth cows from his belly and fashioned them from his two sides. || 43 ||
And from his two feet [issued] horses together with elephants, donkeys, gayals, deer, camels, mules, and likewise other species of animals. || 44 ||
Herbs with fruits and roots were produced from his body hairs.
Having thus created the sacrificial animals together with their bonds, the Lord employed them in the sacrifice. || 45 ||
Therefore, at the beginning of the eon, at the onset of the Tretā Yuga, there were then cows, goats, humans, rams, as well as horses, mules, and donkeys; || 46 ||
These they call domestic animals; now learn of those that are wild!
(cf. 3. Kap.
cf. 3. Kap.
"Beasts of prey, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys, and birds as the fifth [constitute the group]. || 47 ||
Domestic animals are sixfold, while reptiles are sevenfold:
buffaloes, gayals, camels, monkeys, śarabhas, and wolves;
the lion is the seventh among them—these are remembered as the wild animals.
The Gāyatrī meter, the Ṛgveda hymn, the Trivṛt stoma, and the Rathantara [Sāman]. || 49 ||
And from his first mouth, he fashioned the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices,
as well as the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh meter, and the fifteen-fold Stoma.
From his right mouth, he emitted the Bṛhat Sāman as well as the Uktha;
likewise, from it he produced the Sāmans, the Jagatī metre, and the seventeen-fold Stoma.
From his western mouth, he created the Vairūpya, the Atirātra,
the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvans, and the Āptoryāma.
From his northern mouth, he created the Anuṣṭubh meter along with the Svarāja chant,
as well as lightning, thunderbolts, clouds, and red-hued rainbows.
In the beginning of the kalpa, the Lord, the Master, created the vital breaths;
he fashioned the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas for the perfection of sacrifice.
From his limbs, beings of high and low status were born.
For when Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, was engaged in the creation of offspring, he first created a fourfold progeny: the gods, asuras, ancestors, and human beings. || 55 ||
Then he created all beings, both stationary and moving—yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, and likewise the hosts of apsarases. || 56 ||

Hell-beings, kinnaras, and rakṣasas; birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, and serpents; that which is imperishable and that which is perishable—indeed, all this that is both stationary and moving. || 57 ||
Whatever actions those beings performed in a previous creation, those very same actions they undertake again and again as they are created anew.

The violent toward the violent, the mild toward the mild, the cruel toward the cruel, the righteous toward the righteous, the untruthful toward the untruthful—impregnated by those very qualities, they enter [into new births]; therefore, that which is pleasing to each becomes their preference. || 59 ||
The Creator himself ordained the diversity among the great elements, the objects of the senses, and physical forms, as well as the specific functions of the elements. || 60 ||
Some men declare that human effort is the cause of actions; others, O Brahmins, say it is fate; while those who contemplate the elements say it is inherent nature. || 61 ||
They know that human effort and destiny, by virtue of their nature as the fruition of results, are neither identical nor separate, nor is one superior to the other. (62)
Thus, those established in being and possessing equal vision declare that these objects situated in action are neither one, nor both, nor even neither. || 63 ||
That Great Lord created the names and forms of beings, both those already formed and those yet to be manifested, from the very words of the Veda. || 64 ||
Whatever names belong to the sages and whatever insights are found in the Vedas, he bestows those very things upon them as they are born at the end of the night. || 65 ||
Just as the various seasonal signs appear in their recurring cycle according to the season,
so too do those very same things appear at the beginnings of the ages.
Such creations of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
are seen at the end of the night, having resorted to his mental power.
Thus were the beings created, both the stationary and the moving.
When those creatures created by that wise one did not multiply, || 66 ||
Then he created other mental sons who were like himself:
Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and likewise Āṅgirasa.
Marīci, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha, who was born of his mind—these are determined in the Purāṇas to be the nine Brahmās. || 66 ||
cf. Chapter 5, verses 32–33;
cf. Chapter 7.
Śloka 64–66.
Of all those proponents of Brahman, who indeed have Brahman as their self... [663]
Then Brahmā again created Rudra, who was born from his own wrath, as well as Saṃkalpa and Dharma, the progenitor even of the ancients.
In the beginning, Brahmā indeed created from his own mind these beings equal to himself.
The wise one, together with Sanandana, Sanaka, and Sanātana, as well as the all-pervading Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and Sanandana. || 665 ||
They do not cling to the worlds, being independent and eternal;
for they have all attained knowledge, are free from passion, and are devoid of envy. || 666 ||
While they were thus indifferent, the blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, the Supreme Abider, reflected out of conformity with worldly custom: || 667 ||
From his wrath there arose a man with the brilliance of the sun, having the body of a man and a woman, blazing like fire with his splendor. || 67 ||
"Everything has become composed of splendor, possessing a brilliance equal to that of the sun.
Having said, "Divide yourself," he vanished right there. || 671 ||

Having spoken thus, he became twofold: a woman and a man, each separate. He himself was [composed of] half of eleven; that Supreme Lord was born as elevenfold, having established himself as half of his own self.
Then he spoke to all those great-souled ones, who were desirous of the welfare of the world, concerning its expansion: || 681 ||
Indeed, for the sake of the world's affairs, you must strive with unwearied diligence for the establishment and the welfare of the entire universe and all its inhabitants. || 682 ||
Thus addressed, they wept and fled in all directions; because of their weeping and fleeing, they became renowned by the name "Rudras. || 683 ||
For those by whom this entire triple world, with its moving and unmoving beings, is pervaded—they are unsurpassed in the world, the ultimate refuge for all worlds;
possessing the strength of many tens of thousands of nāgas, these lords of the hosts are truly valiant. || 684 ||

In that regard, she who was previously mentioned to you by me as the highly fortunate Great Goddess, forming half the body of Śaṅkara—that very woman, Satī, has indeed become [this one] here; she is the woman who emerged from the mouth of the Self-Existent One. || 69 ||
The Goddess, for the welfare of the worlds, was propitiated by Dakṣa in ancient times. || 69 ||
"Her right half of the body is white and her left is likewise black;
divide yourself," thus was the Goddess addressed by the Self-born One. (70)
O twice-born ones, that [speech] which has been described is indeed twofold: white and black.
I shall state its various names; listen with full concentration. (71)
Svāhā, Svadhā, Mahāvidyā, Medhā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī;
Satī, Dākṣāyaṇī, Vidyā, Icchā, Śakti, Kriyātmikā;
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā. (72)
Umā Haimavatī, Śaṣṭhī, Kalyāṇī, and Ekamātṛkā; she who is renowned as Prajñā and Mahābhāgā is celebrated in the world as Gaurī. (73)
Gaṇāmbikā, Mahādevī, Nandinī, Jātavedasī,
Sāvitrī, Varadā, Puṇyā, Pāvanī, Lokaviśrutā,
Ājñā, Āveśanī, Kṛṣṇā, Tāmasī, Sāttvikī, and Śivā. || 73 ||
Now hear in brief, according to the facts and in proper sequence, how Viśvarūpa [arose] from the noble lady through the manifestation of her body as distinct [forms]:
Prakṛti, Vikṛtā, Raudrī, Durgā, Bhadrā, and Pramāthinī. (74)
Kālarātri, Mahāmāyā, Revatī, and Bhūtanāyikā—
these, O observers of good vows, are the names of the Goddess during the transformations at the end of the Dvāpara age:
Gautamī, Kauśikī, Āryā, Caṇḍī, Kātyāyanī, and Satī.
The maiden, the goddess of the Yādavas, the bestower of boons, dark-brown as a black bee;
she whose banner bears a peacock, who wields the trident, the supreme practitioner of celibacy;
the sister of Mahendra and Upendra, both the daughter of Mahendra and the sister of Indra.
On the Dṛṣadvatī [he is] the bearer of the single trident; Vṛṣa and Kanyā are the two garments.
Aparājitā, Bahubhujā, Pragalbhā, Siṃhavāhinī, and the slayer of the Daityas such as Śumbha; Ekānaṃsā, the slayer of Daityas,
Mahāmahiṣamardinī, Māyā, and Mahiṣamardinī.
Amoghā, whose abode is the Vindhya mountains, the valiant leader of the Gaṇas. || 77 ||
These names of the goddesses, which are free from modification, have been declared by me in due order as the true names of the goddess Bhadrakālī. || 78 ||
Those men who recite this, for them there is no defeat—whether in the forest, on a mountain, in a city, or even in a house. || 79 ||
One should employ this protection whether in water or on land, against tigers, crocodiles, and thieves, and especially in haunted places. 80.
Furthermore, in all afflictions, one should recite the names of the Goddess, as well as those of the child-seizing spirits, elemental ghosts, and the Pūtana mothers. (81)
One should employ this protection for children who are being oppressed.
Within the family of Mahādevī, two [deities] are celebrated as Prajñā and Śrī;
from these two come thousands of goddesses, by whom the entire world is pervaded. || 82 ||
At the beginning of the Kalpa, he emitted Resolve (saṃkalpa) and Purposeful Exertion (vyavasāya), which brings happiness to all beings; these were born from the Unmanifest source. || 82 ||
And the son of Brahmā known as Ruci was born of his mind; from his breath he created Dakṣa, and from his two eyes Marīci. || 82 ||
But the sage Bhṛgu was born from the heart of the one born from the waters.
From his head [he created] Aṅgiras, and likewise from his ear, Atri. || 82 ||
From Udāna he likewise created Pulastya, and from Vyāna, Pulaha;
from Samāna he produced Vasiṣṭha, and from Apāna he fashioned Kratu. || 82 ||
He created the auspicious Nīlalohita, whose nature is self-conceit (abhimāna).
Thus, these twelve sons of Brahmā are known as those born from his vital breaths (prāṇaja). || 82 ||
Thus, these should be known as the mind-born sons of Brahmā;
whereas those beginning with Bhṛgu, who were created [later], are these nine exponents of the Veda (brahmavādins).
They were the ancient householders; by them, Dharma was first set in motion.
These twelve, together with Rudra, indeed bring forth progeny. || 82 ||
Rbhu and Sanatkumāra—these two are of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas);
they were born earlier than them all, being the first-born of all. || 82 ||
When the first ancient kalpa had passed, those two, the accomplishers of the world, remained in the Vairāja world, having withdrawn their splendor within themselves. || 82 ||

Having established themselves in the dharma of yoga by fixing their own selves within the Self, those two of great luster should carry out the duty toward their subjects as well as the pursuit of desire. || 82 ||
As it was born, so indeed is it called here "Kumāra"; therefore, this name "Sanatkumāra" has been proclaimed for him. (7.67–614) || 8211 ||
Those twelve lineages of theirs were divine, endowed with celestial qualities,
characterized by ritual action, possessed of progeny, and adorned by great seers.
Thus was this world, produced from the instruments [of creation], created by the self-existent Svayambhū.
The transformation, beginning with the Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), arises spontaneously from Prakṛti. || 8213 ||
They possess the light and radiance of the moon and sun, adorned with planets and constellations,
and are encompassed by rivers, oceans, and mountains.
And with various kinds of cities and likewise with joyful provinces, Brahmā dwells through the nights in that unmanifest Brahma-forest. || 8215 ||
Originating from the seed of the Unmanifest and arising through its very grace, it consists of the trunk of the intellect (*buddhi*), with the sense-faculties as its hollow sprouts. (8216)

It has the great elements as its branches, is possessed of leaves through various distinctions, has dharma and adharma as its beautiful flowers, and yields the arising of the fruits of pleasure and pain. (8217)
This eternal tree is the livelihood of all beings;
it is indeed the forest of Brahman belonging to that very tree of Brahman.

That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent—this is the favoring creation (anugraha-sarga), which is the primordial (prākṛta) creation of Brahmā. || 8219 ||
But the six emanations beginning with the Principal (Mukhya) were modified and preceded by intelligence;
they came into being throughout the three periods of time as the self-conceited forms of Brahmā. || 8220 ||
Furthermore, those emanations are remembered by the wise as being mutual causes for one another.
There are two divine birds, yoked together, with branches and leaves of gold and coral;
yet only one knows the tree, and no other does, because he is the Self of all. || 8221 ||
The sages praise heaven as his head,
the sky as his navel, and the moon and sun as his two eyes;
the quarters are his ears, and the earth is his feet.
He is the inconceivable self, the source of all beings. || 8222 ||
From his mouth were born the Brāhmaṇas;
from the front part of his chest came the Kṣatriyas;
from his thighs the Vaiśyas; and from his feet the Śūdras.
All social classes have emerged from his body.
Maheśvara is beyond the unmanifest; the cosmic egg is born from the unmanifest.
From the egg, Brahmā was again born, by whom these worlds were created. || 8224 ||

**Section 1: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter 7** Sūta said: [Rudra, Dharma, Manas,] as well as Ruci and Akṛti, ... (The text continues with the names of the progenitors and their respective wives. ... Sūta said: [From these were born the Manus and the Prajāpatis. ... Sūta said: "O Brahmins, I shall now describe the secondary creation (*pratisarga*) in detail, as it occurred in the past. Listen attentively. When the world was entirely dissolved into darkness and lay submerged in water, the Lord, having assumed the form of a boar, raised up the earth. Sūta said: "The earth was then covered by the waters of the ocean. Having lifted her up, he established her upon the foundation of the waters. Then, desiring to create all beings, the Self-born One first created the waters alone. From the waters, he produced fire; from fire, he produced wind; and from wind, he produced space. Space, wind, fire, water, and earth—these are the five elements (*bhūtas*). Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the five qualities (*guṇas*) of the elements. Ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the five organs of perception (*buddhīndriyas*). Foot, hand, organ of excretion, organ of generation, and organ of speech are the five organs of action (*karmendriyas*). Mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), and the great principle (*mahat*)—these are the four internal faculties (*antaḥkaraṇas*). Thus, the twenty-four principles have been enumerated. He who knows them truly is not reborn. Sūta said: "Then, O best of Brahmins, the Self-born One created the seven worlds, beginning with the Earth, along with their respective inhabitants. He created the mountains, the rivers, the oceans, the forests, and the various types of trees. He created the gods, the demons, the *gandharvas*, the *yakṣas*, the *rākṣasas*, the serpents, and human beings. He created the four castes (*varṇas*) and the four stages of life (*āśramas*), as well as the duties (*dharmas*) prescribed for each. He created the Vedas, the sacrificial rites, the rules of conduct, and the various forms of austerity. Thus, the entire universe, consisting of both the moving and the non-moving, was brought forth by the Great-Souled One. Sūta said: "I shall now describe the dissolution (*pralaya*) of the world, which occurs at the end of a Kalpa. Listen with focused attention. When the time for dissolution arrives, the Great-Souled One withdraws the entire universe into himself. First, the earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into wind; and wind dissolves into space. Space dissolves into the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*); the ego-consciousness dissolves into the intellect (*buddhi*); and the intellect dissolves into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). The Unmanifest, which is the source of all, then dissolves into the Supreme Soul. This is the dissolution of the world, occurring at the end of a Kalpa. After this, the world remains in a state of equilibrium, devoid of distinctions, until the next cycle of creation begins. "These nine Brahmās are established as certain in the Purāṇa, for all of them are self-born from the Self-existent Brahmā, who is the master of his own self. || 66 ||

For unrighteousness consists of moving against the current, and violence is of an impure nature.

She stands pervading both heaven and earth with her majesty;

But that female half who was created was born as Śatarūpā;

A period of seventy-one yugas is here called a manvantara.

His two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, were the best among those who possess sons;

Prāṇa should be known as Dakṣa, and Saṃkalpa is called Manu;

Faith, Fortune, Fortitude, Contentment, Nourishment, Intelligence, Action, likewise Understanding, Modesty, Form, Peace, Success, and Fame as the thirteenth; || 24 ||

Śraddhā indeed gave birth to Kāma; Darpas is remembered as the son of Lakṣmī.

[He saw] those who were tawny, carrying quivers, wearing matted hair, and very red;

Those of great form, those of deformed form, and those of manifold forms among the embodied;

Shining brightly and emitting smoke. || 50 ||

## Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter Eight (Bd. I. 10.1–88; Vā.
27.1–60) The Sages said (the Seer said):
"In this *kalpa*, the manifestation of the Great-Souled One has not been mentioned by you."
Together with the sages who were practitioners of Mahādeva Rudra. || 1 ||
Sūta said:
I have briefly described the origin of the primary creation;
I shall now speak of its details, including the names [of the deities] along with their respective forms. || 2 ||
Mahādeva begot many sons upon his wives;
though other kalpas have passed, hear now of them in this present kalpa! || 3 ||
At the beginning of the kalpa, as the Lord meditated upon a son equal to himself, there appeared from his *ūka* a youth who was blue and red. || 4 ||
He wept with a loud and terrible voice, as if burning everything with his splendor.
Seeing the youth Nīlalohita suddenly weeping, [he was struck with wonder]. || 5 ||
"Why do you weep, O youth? Brahmā replied to him.
He said: "O Grandfather, give me my first name! (6)
"O God, you are Rudra by name! When he was addressed thus, he wept again. To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke once more: "Why do you weep? (7)
"Give me a second name! he said to the Self-Existent One.
"You shall be Bhava by name, O God! When thus addressed, he wept again. || 8 ||
To him who was weeping, Brahmā replied, "Why do you weep? Being thus addressed, he replied to him: "Give me a third name! || 9 ||
"You are Śarva by name, O God! When he was addressed thus, he wept again.
To him as he wept, Brahmā spoke once more: "Why do you weep? || 10 ||
"Give me a fourth name! When he was thus addressed, he spoke again: "O God, you are Īśāna by name! When he was thus addressed, he wept once more. || 11 ||
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke again: "Why do you weep? He replied to the Self-born One: "Give me a fifth name! (12)
"O God, you are the lord of animals!"—when he was thus addressed, he wept again.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke once more: "Why do you weep? || 13 ||
"Give me a sixth name," he replied to the Self-Existent One;
"O God, you are named Bhīma! Having been addressed thus, he wept again. || 14 ||
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke again:
"Give me a seventh name! Being thus addressed, he replied to him: || 15 ||
"You are Ugra by name, O God!"—when he was addressed thus, he wept again.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke once more: "Why do you weep? (16)
"O Lord, give me an eighth name! he spoke again. Mahādeva, having been addressed thus, said, "You are 'Api' by name," and then became silent. || 17 ||
Having received these names from Brahmā, Nīlalohita said, "Please assign the locations for these names! || 18 ||
Then, these names were released by the Self-Existent One for them.
The sun, water, earth, fire, wind, and space as well. || 19 ||
O Moon, the initiated Brahmin is thus your body in eight forms;
among them, you should be honored, saluted, and respectfully paid homage.
Brahmā spoke again to that youth Nīlalohita:
"O All-pervading Lord, as for what was previously said by me to you—that your name is indeed Rudra—" || 21 ||
"Of you, the first-born, the Sun is the first body by name.
When this was said, that which was his illuminating splendor became the eye. || 22 ||
He entered that very sun; therefore, he is remembered as Rudra.
One should avoid looking at the sun when it is rising or setting. || 23 ||
Since it is born perpetually and since it stands eternally, one who desires long life and remains ever pure should not look at the sun. || 24 ||
For the Brahmins cause Rudra, who is both past and future, to swell with strength as they attend upon the two twilights, chanting the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajus verses. || 25 ||
Rising, he remains among the Ṛg-verses at midday, and then among the Yajus-formulas;
furthermore, in the afternoon, Rudra enters among the Sāman-chants in due order. || 26 ||
Therefore, one should never urinate toward Rudra, whether he has risen or has indeed set, under any circumstances whatsoever. || 27 ||
The god Rudra does not indeed harm those twice-born ones who are thus disciplined.
Then Brahmā spoke again to that god Nīlalohita: || 28 ||
This second name which has been proclaimed for you by me, "Bhava"—let this water be your second body by name. || 29 ||
When this had been said, that which was the essence consisting of rasa residing in his body entered those waters; therefore, water is known as Bhava. || 30 ||
Because beings arise from them and are brought into being by them, existence (bhava) is so called due to the very arising and bringing into being of beings. || 31 ||
Therefore, one should never void urine or excrement in water;
nor should one spit, nor plunge into it, nor bathe in water while naked, nor engage in sexual intercourse [therein]. One should never spit [in water]. || 32 ||
One should never engage in sexual intercourse and should avoid bathing the head; nor should one look at these women while they are carrying water, even when they are standing still. || 33 ||
These bodies of water are considered by the sages to be both pure and impure because their forms consist of both pure and impure substances; yet the waters themselves are never defiled.
One should, however, avoid those that are discolored, tasteless, foul-smelling, or scanty. || 34 ||
The ocean is indeed the womb of the waters; therefore, they desire it.
For the waters become pure and immortal once they have reached the sea. || 35 ||
Therefore, one should not obstruct the waters; they long for the ocean.
The divine Bhava does not harm him who always conducts himself thus with regard to the waters. || 36 ||
Then Brahmā spoke again to the youth Nīlalohita:
"O All-pervading Lord, as for that third name of yours which was uttered by me as 'Śarva'... (37)
"Let this earth be his third body, named Tanu.
When this was said, that which was stable in his body, known as the bones, [remained]. || 38 ||
He then entered the earth, because of which the earth is called Śarvā;
therefore, one should not void excrement or urine on ploughed land. || 39 ||
One should not urinate in the shade, nor on a path, nor in one's own clear shadow; having covered the head and having concealed the ground with grass, one should do so. || 40 ||
"Whoever conducts himself thus upon the earth, Śarva will certainly not harm him.
Then Brahmā spoke again to the youth Nilalohita: || 41 ||
That which was declared by me as your fourth name, "Īśāna," shall have its fourth [vowel] as its fourth [syllable]; Vāyu shall be your body by name. || 42 ||
When this was said, that wind which resides within the body and is designated as the fivefold *prāṇa* entered him; by means of that, he became the Lord of Wind (*Māruta*). || 43 ||
Therefore, one should not revile this wind, the lord who has departed;
for those who serve him indeed conduct their sacrifices through him. || 44 ||
"In this manner, Maheśāna does not harm that god at all.
Then Brahmā spoke again to that god Dhūmralohita: || 45 ||
That which was indeed called the fifth by me as "Paśupati," let this fifth body of the fifth [Lord] be named Agni for you. || 46 ||
When this was said, that heat residing within his body, known as warmth, then entered the fire; therefore, he is indeed Paśupati. || 47 ||
Since Agni was once a sacrificial animal and since he protects animals, therefore Agni is declared to be the body of that Paśupati. || 48 ||
Therefore, one should not burn impure things, nor heat one's feet [over it];
one should not place it beneath oneself, nor step over it. || 49 ||
"Even the god Paśupati will not harm one who is thus disciplined.
Then Brahmā spoke again to that Śvetapiṅgala god: || 50 ||
"O Lord, as for that sixth name 'Bhīma' which has been proclaimed by me for you, let the sky be the body for that sixth name. || 51 ||
When this was said, that which had been the hollow space within his body entered the ether; from that, Bhīma’s body [was restored]. || 52 ||
Since the deity is remembered to be in the sky, one should never void urine or feces there, nor eat, nor drink while uncovered. (53)
One should neither engage in sexual intercourse nor cast away food remnants;
the Lord does not harm him who conducts himself thus in this formidable place. || 54 ||
Then Brahmā spoke again to that powerful lord god:
"O Lord, as for the seventh name which was uttered by me, 'Aghora' is yours. || 55 ||
From his name, a slender body of yours becomes a twice-born man initiated for sacrifice.
When this has been said, that consciousness of his which resides within the body— || 56 ||
He indeed entered that initiated Brāhmaṇa who was a performer of the Soma sacrifice;
for that duration of time, the initiated Brāhmaṇa was remembered as the fierce deity. || 57 ||
Therefore, one should not revile this [person], nor should one speak ill of their reputation;
for those who indeed revile them take away their own evil. || 58 ||
The fierce god does not indeed harm those twice-born ones who are thus disciplined.
Then Brahmā spoke again to that god, who possesses the brilliance of the sun: || 59 ||
That which was declared by me to you as the eighth name, "Mahādeva"—may the moon be the physical embodiment of that eighth name for you. || 60 ||
When this had been said, that mind which was the volitional faculty of the Lord entered the Moon; from that, Mahādeva became the Moon. || 61 ||
Therefore, this great god Candramas is indeed manifested [therein].
On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), a twice-born man must certainly not cut trees, shrubs, or medicinal herbs. || 62 ||
Soma is known as Mahādeva, for the multitude of medicinal herbs is indeed his very self.
Thus, the wise man who conducts himself in this manner at every sacred festival (parvan), || 63 ||
Mahādeva does not harm him who knows that Lord in this way.
By day the sun protects the subjects, but by night it is the moon. || 64 ||
Both the sun and the moon may meet for a single night;
however, on the night of the new moon, one should always dwell in union with that [truth]. || 65 ||
All this is pervaded by Rudra through his bodies and his names;
he who moves alone is this very Sun, and he is called Rudra. (66)
That which living beings behold with their eyes through the light of the sun is Rudra, established as the white-souled one, who drinks the water with his rays. || 67 ||
It is indeed eaten and drunk out of a desire for food, drink, and the like;
that body, born of water, is accumulated within the physical frames themselves. || 68 ||

By means of his stabilized splendor, he sustains all creatures; that earthly body of his, belonging to Śarva, supports all beings. (69)
That which abides within the bodies of beings through the functions of the vital breaths, consisting of air and belonging to Īśāna, is the *prāṇa* of living creatures here. || 70 ||
That subtle body belonging to him which digests yellow and white foods within the bellies of living beings is called the Pāśupata; that fire is called the "Cooker. || 71 ||
Those cavities that exist here within the bodies for the purpose of the movement of the vital air—this is declared to be the formidable body. || 72 ||

The state of those who have been initiated for the Vaitāna sacrifice and other rites, who are exponents of Brahman, is indeed a fierce form; therefore, such an initiate is known as "Ugra" (the Fierce). || 73 ||
That which was his faculty of volition is established here among living beings;
that mental body of his exists as the moon within all creatures. || 74 ||
For he becomes ever new as he is born again and again;
he is drunk at the proper time by the wise together with the ancestors. || 75 ||
That Mahādeva is of the nature of immortality; he is remembered as the Moon, consisting of water.
Of him, that first form which is proclaimed by the name Raudrī— || 76 ||
His wife was Suvarcas, and her son was Śanaiścara.
Bhava’s second wife, however, is known by the name Āpa, who is his body. || 77 ||
His wife is remembered as Oṣātrā, and his son is remembered as Uśanas;
she who is the third of all is known by the name Bhūmis-tanu. || 78 ||
His wife was Vikeśitī, and his son is known as Aṅgāraka. As for the body which belongs to the fourth [face], Īśāna, it is called Vāta by name. || 79 ||
His wife was named Śivā, and her son was Manojava;
Avijñātagati was the second of the two sons of Anila. || 80 ||
That form of Pāśupati which is known by the twice-born as Agni has Svāhā as his wife, and Skanda is known as his son. || 81 ||
The sixth [son]’s formidable body is called Ākāśa by name;
the quarters are remembered as his wives, and Heaven is remembered as his son. || 82 ||
The fierce body is the seventh direction; it is traditionally held that the initiated Brahmin is [that direction], initiation is known as the wife, and their offspring is called the son. || 83 ||
That which is known as the body of the great eighth [planet] by name is remembered as the Moon;
Rohiṇī is indeed his wife, and Budha is remembered as his son. || 84 ||
Thus these forms of his have been proclaimed together with their names; indeed, among those forms, he is to be praised and saluted according to each respective name.

Likewise, he is worshipped with devotion by his devotees in the sun, in the waters, in the earth, as well as in the wind, in fire, in the sky, and in the quarters; likewise, he is to be saluted with devotion by name in the moon. || 86 ||
Thus, the man who knows that God through His forms and names becomes possessed of progeny; indeed, he attains union with the Lord. 87.
Thus has this secret glory of Bhīma been proclaimed by me to you;
may there be constant welfare for our bipeds, and may there be welfare for our quadrupeds. || 88 ||
This diagnosis of the bodily humors has been declared along with their names;
now listen, O progeny of Bhṛgu, to that of the god Mahādeva! (89)

**Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter Nine** Then Khyāti bore to Bhṛgu two lords over pleasure and pain, who bestow the auspicious and the inauspicious upon all living beings here on earth. (1)
The two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ wander through the Manvantaras;
their elder sister is the goddess Śrī, the creator of the worlds. || 2 ||

That beautiful woman, having obtained the god Nārāyaṇa as her husband, gave birth to two sons who were the offspring of Nārāyaṇa: Bala and Unmāda. [The son of Bala was Tejas, while the son of Unmāda was Saṃśaya. || 3 ||
He had other mind-born sons who move through the sky;
they carry the celestial chariots of the gods of meritorious deeds. || 4 ||
O daughter of Meru, Smṛti was the wife of both Vidhātṛ and Dhātṛ;
Āyati and Niyati were their two sons, both firm in their vows.
Prāṇa and Mṛkaṇḍu were the two eternal repositories of the Veda.
From Mṛkaṇḍu and Manasvinī, Mārkaṇḍeya was indeed born. || 6 ||
His son Vedaśīra was born of Dhūmapatnī. From Vedaśīra, sons were born of Pīvarī who are remembered as the founders of lineages;
they are known as the Mārkaṇḍeyas, sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas. || 7 ||
To Prāṇa, in Puṇḍarīkā, was born a son named Dyutimat;
and to Dyutimat were born both Unnata and Svanavāta. || 8 ||
The sons and grandsons of those two Bhārgavas [fought] with one another. Now that the Svāyambhuva Manvantara has passed, hear about the progeny of Marīci! (9)
Marīci’s wife, Saṃbhūti, gave birth to the Prajāpati Pūrṇamāsa, who was born of her own self, as well as these daughters; learn of them now. || 10 ||
Kṛṣṭi, Pr̥ṣti, and likewise Iṣa and the auspicious Apaciti—these two sons Pūrṇamāsa begot upon Sarasvatī. || 11 ||
Both of them were Virajas and Dharmiṣṭha, as well as Parvasan.
The son of Virajas was the learned and renowned Sudhāman. || 12 ||
That Sudhāmā, the son of Vairāja, a world-protector of virtuous soul and the powerful son of Gaurī, is established in the eastern direction. || 13 ||
Having entered into all the hosts of the Parvas, that highly illustrious one indeed begot two sons, Parva and Parvasāyana. || 14 ||
And Yajñavāma, the wise son of Kāśyapa—of these two, sons were born who established their respective lineages and were resolved upon renunciation. || 15 ||
Smṛti was the wife of Aṅgiras; she gave birth to those two sons born of her own self, as well as four meritorious daughters who were world-renowned: || 16 ||
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and likewise Anumati;
and similarly Bharata and Agni, both of them renowned. || 17 ||
Sadvatī gave birth to Parjanya, the powerful son of Agni.
Parjanya, whose hair is golden, was born of Mārīcī;
he is indeed remembered as a world-protector who remains until the dissolution of all beings. || 18 ||
From Kīrtimant were born Dhenuka and Tāva; both were stainless, possessed of great resolve, and were the best among the descendants of Aṅgiras. || 19 ||
Their sons and grandsons have indeed passed away by the thousands;
Anasūyā, being free from blemish, gave birth to five sons of Atri.
And his daughter was named Śruti, who was the mother of Śaṅkhapada;
she was the wife of Kardama, the patriarch of the Paulaha lineage. || 21 ||
Satyanetra, Havya, Āpomūrti, Śanaiścara,
and Soma as the fifth— these were the [sons] during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Together with Yāmadēva, these are proclaimed as the five Ātreyas who have passed away;
their sons and grandsons are the descendants of those high-souled Ātreyas. || 23 ||
In the past Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, there were hundreds and thousands [of them];
Dattoli was born as the son of Pulastya by his wife Prīti. || 24 ||
In his previous birth during the Svāyambhuva interval, he was known as Agastya;
Madhyama, Devabāhu, and Vinīta—these three were [his brothers]. || 25 ||
The youngest sister among them was renowned by the name Sadvatī;
she was the radiant mother of Parjanya, and the auspicious Śubhā is remembered as the wife of Agni. || 26 ||
And the wife of the wise sage Dattola, son of Paulastya and born of affection, Sujaṅghī, gave birth to many sons. || 27 ||
They are celebrated as the Paulastyas, remembered [as having appeared] during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Kṣamā, however, gave birth to sons for the patriarch Pulaha. || 28 ||
All of them possessed the splendor of the three sacrificial fires, and their fame was firmly established;
these three were Kardama, Ūrvarīvant, and Sahiṣṇu. (29)
The sage Vanakapivān, the auspicious maiden Pīvarī, and Śruti, the wife of Kardama and daughter of Atri, themselves gave birth to [these]: || 30 ||
A son named Śaṅkhapada and likewise a daughter named Kāmyā.
That illustrious Śaṅkhapada was indeed a world-protector (lokapāla) and a lord of progeny (prajāpati). || 31 ||
In the southern direction, Rata was given to Priyavrata as a wife.
From Priyavrata, Kāmyā obtained sons equal to Svāyambhuva Manu.
And there were ten pairs of daughters, by whom the Kṣatriya race was propagated;
[his] son was the famous Dhanaka, whose other names were Pīvaṃś and Sahiṣṇu. || 33 ||
The slender-waisted Yaśodharā gave birth to Kāmadeva;
the auspicious Saṃnatī bore sons equal to Kratu from Kratu. || 34 ||
They have neither wives nor sons, for all of them are perpetual celibates;
these sixty thousand are known as the Vālakhilyas. || 35 ||
They go before Aruṇa, surrounding the sun;
until the dissolution of all beings, they all remain companions to the winged one. || 36 ||
Your two younger sisters, Puṇyā and Satyavatī,
are indeed the daughters-in-law of Parvaṇi, the son of Pūrṇamāsa.
In Ūrjā, seven sons were indeed born to Vasiṣṭha;
and their elder sister was Puṇḍarīkā, who possessed a slender waist. || 38 ||
She was the mother of the radiant Prāṇa and his beloved queen;
and her younger brothers were the seven famous Vāsiṣṭhas. || 39 ||
Raja, Gartodhvabahu, Savana, Pavana, Sutapas, and Śukla—these are all remembered as the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis). || 40 ||
Moreover, the illustrious Mārkaṇḍeyī gave birth to Rajas, the king and lord of creatures (prajāpati), known as Ketumān, in the western quarter. || 41 ||
The lineages by name of those high-souled Vāsiṣṭhas who passed away in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara have been told; now hear about the progeny of Agni! 42.
Thus has this creation of the sages been proclaimed along with its subsequent lineages; hereafter, I shall describe the lineage of Agni in detail and in due order.
That Agni who was known as the presiding deity during the Svāyambhuva interval,
being the mind-born son of Brahmā, from him Svāhā was born.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and that which is known as Śuci Agni:
Pavamāna is produced by friction, while Pāvaka is said to be of lightning origin. || 45 ||
Śuci is to be known as the son of Sūrya; those three, however, are the sons of Svāhā.
Nirmathya is Pavamāna, while Śuci is remembered as the son of Sūrya. || 46 ||
The Abhyagni and the Vaidyuta—these indeed are their stations.
And the son of Pavamāna is called Kavyavāhana. || 47 ||
Pāvaki, however, was together with Rakṣas; Havyavāha was the son of Śuci.
Agni is the carrier of oblations for the gods, and Kavyavāhana is [the carrier] for the ancestors. || 48 ||
Saharakṣas was the son of the Asuras; these were the three fires of those three [sages].
Their sons and grandsons, however, numbered exactly forty-nine. || 49 ||
I shall describe their individual classification by name:
the first is the world-renowned Laukika fire, the son of Brahmā. || 50 ||
Brahmodana was his son, renowned by the name Bharata;
Vaiśvānara was his son, who carried the sacrificial oblation for a hundred years.
Formerly, Amṛta was churned by Atharvan in the Puṣkara ocean;
that Atharvan is the worldly fire, while Dadhyañc is the son of Atharvan. || 52 ||
Atharvan is to be known as Bhṛgu; indeed, the Aṅgirasas are remembered as the descendants of Atharvan.
Therefore, that is the common (laukika) fire, which is considered the Dadhyaṅga of Atharvan. || 53 ||
Furthermore, that Pavamāna who is remembered by the sages as being produced by friction is to be known as the Gārhapatya fire; two sons of his are recorded. || 54 ||
The fire to be praised is the Āhavanīya, remembered as the bearer of oblations;
the second is declared to be the son, the Śukra fire which is led forward. (55)
Likewise, both Śaṃsyā and Agni’s daughter Apasavyā were born.
Śaṃsyā, however, was desired by Havyavāhana as his sixteen wives. || 56 ||
That fire which is the Āhavanīya, known by the twice-born as its presiding deity, [is present] in the Kāverī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Narmadā, and likewise the Yamunā. (57)
The Godāvarī, the Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, the Irāvatī, the Vipāśā, the Kauśikī, as well as the Śatadrū and the Sarayū; || 58 ||
Having divided himself into sixteen parts— namely Sītā, Sarasvatī, Hlādinī, and Pāvanī— he distributed them among those rivers individually.
He divided himself; he became the *dhiṣṇīs* among them.
The *dhiṣṇī* that moves through the Kṛttikās was [the first]; from that *dhiṣṇī* were born those who do not deviate [from it], and they are the *dhiṣṇayas*. Those *dhiṣṇayas* were born among them.
Because they were born from the *dhiṣṇīs*, they are celebrated as the *Dhiṣṇyas*.
Thus, these sons of the rivers were indeed born from the *dhiṣṇīs* themselves. || 61 ||
Listen with full attention as I describe, exactly as they are, those fires which are to be maintained and those which are to be attended to by them. (62)

Vibhu is the *agnīdh*, and the other *dhiṣṇya* hearths situated there are prescribed according to their respective places, in sequence, during the *savana* on the day of the Soma-pressing (*sautya-aha*). || 63 ||
Listen to the sequence of the fires that are indescribable and inexpressible:
the Samrāj fire is Kṛśānu, who is the second, situated within the altar. || 64 ||
The sovereign [king] worships those eight twice-born ones who have Agni as their mouth;
he is designated as the second member of the assembly, namely Pavamāna. || 65 ||
That which is called the sky is perceived as the *pratakkā* at the crossroads;
for from that, the sacrificial offering (*havya*), when not yet cleansed, is perceived in the *śāmitra* fire.
Ṛtudhāman and Sujyotis are proclaimed as belonging to the Audumbarī;
Viśvavyacas, Samudra, and Agni are proclaimed in the station of Brahman. || 67 ||
He who is named Vasu, the light of Brahman, is said to be in the place of Brahman;
he is to be worshipped as Aja-ekapāt, and he is indeed the Śālāmukhīya fire. || 68 ||
For that Agni Ahirbudhnya is remembered as one who is not to be designated [as a guest], yet he is known as the Lord of the House (Gṛhapati).
All these sons of Śaṃsyā are remembered as those to be approached with reverence by the twice-born. || 69 ||
Next, I shall describe those who are to dwell there, as well as his eight sons:
Vibhu, Pravāhaṇa, and Agnīdhra; the others are the Dhiṣṇya fires stationed therein.
They are assigned to their respective places in due order during the Soma-pressing on the day of the Sautya sacrifice;
for the fire known as Hotrīya is indeed the Vahni called Havyavāhana. || 71 ||
Praśānta Agni and Pracetas are the names of the second;
thereafter, Agni Vaiśvadeva is called Brahmānācchaṃsin. || 72 ||
Agni is the *uśij*, the seer who is the *potṛ*;
he is manifested as Agni.
Agni is the *āvāri* and the *vābhāri*.
He is perceived as belonging to the Vaiṣṭhīyas. || 73 ||
Avasphūrja is Vivasvat,
and he is also called Āsthāṃś;
the eighth is the fire Sudhyu.
That is called the *mārjālīya*. || 74 ||
For these [fires] are brought from their hearths on the Sutyā day; they are indeed established by means of two [verses].
That [ocean] is known as the womb of the waters, for it is—
The name of the waters is manifested. || 75 ||
Then he who is named Pāvaka is called the womb of the waters; that fire is to be known as the avabhṛtha, and it is offered together with the rite to Varuṇa. || 76 ||
Hṛcchaya was his son; he is indeed the fire that digests the food of men within their bellies.
The learned one, possessing wrath, is known as the son of the digestive fire (Jāṭhara). || 77 ||
That fire, rising up on all sides, would utterly consume all beings here;
yet the son of that wrathful fire is known as the terrible Saṃvartaka. || 78 ||
Drinking the waters, he dwells in the ocean as the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha);
the son of Samudravāsī is known as Saharakṣas. || 79 ||
The son of Saharakṣas is emaciated and burns the houses of men;
his son is Kravyād Agni, who devours dead men. || 80 ||
Thus these sons of the purifying Agni have been proclaimed. Then Śuci, the son of Sūrya, was offered as a libation by the Gandharvas. || 81 ||
That fire which is produced by friction in the forest is indeed the fire that is kindled;
but that which is carried forth is the venerable one named Āyu. || 82 ||
Mahiṣa was the son of Āyu, and his son was named Savana;
that fire which presides over the *pākayajña* sacrifices is known as Savana. || 83 ||
And the son of Savana was Agni Adbhuta, who was of great fame;
and Vivici is recorded as the son of Adbhuta Agni, and he too was great. || 84 ||
One who is conceited regarding expiatory rites always consumes the offered oblation as if it were already sacrificed.
Vivici was indeed the son of Arka, and these [following] are the sons of that Agni: || 85 ||
Aṇikavān, Vājasṛk, Rakṣohā, Pathikṛt, Surabhi, Vasu, and Annāda—whosoever has entered [these], he is Rukmarāj. || 86 ||
For this progeny belongs to Śuci Agni, and there are fourteen Vahnis;
thus these Vahnis have been declared, who are led forward in the sacrifices. || 87 ||
In the primordial creation, during the Svāyambhuva interval, those fires, together with the Yāmas and the best of gods, were indeed the presiding deities (abhimānin). || 88 ||
In this world, among these animate and inanimate objects fit for habitation, there were formerly beings who, dwelling here, took pride in their status as fire-carriers. || 89 ||
Established in these ritual acts within the optional and occasional sacrifices,
they passed away in the previous Manvantara along with Śukra, Yāma, and their sons.
During the first interval of Manu, these were the abodes and the inhabitants by the high-souled and meritorious gods;
thus have these places been described by me.
By those very [calculations], the characteristic of the fires has been enumerated for all past and future Manvantaras as well. || 92 ||
For all these are indeed ascetics, and likewise all are sustainers of the Veda;
they are all remembered as lords of creatures and as luminous beings. || 93 ||
They are to be known as existing throughout all seven Manvantaras, beginning with Svārociṣa and ending with Sāvarṇi, assuming various forms for various purposes.
The present fires exist together with the present gods;
the future fires will exist together with the future gods. || 95 ||
Thus has this collection of fires been enumerated in due order;
furthermore, [the ritual] for the ancestors will be described again in detail and in proper sequence. || 96 ||
